#179360. Flipping a House Isn’t Paying Like It Used To. Is Renting the Better Bet?

Flipping a House Isn’t Paying Like It Used To. Is Renting the Better Bet?

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The typical home flip generated just $60,526 in gross profit in the second quarter of 2026, down from $71,000 a year earlier, according to newly introduced data—before accounting for renovation costs or other expenses.
  • It's a shrinking cushion for investors who have long relied on a simple formula to fuel their business: Buy low, apply elbow grase, and sell high.
  • The report, from real estate data analytics tech giant ATTOM, found that flipping returns have been declining for two years, with the typical gross return falling to 21.5%, from 27.6% a year earlier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The typical home flip generated just $60,526 in gross profit in the second quarter of 2026, down from $71,000 a year earlier, according to newly introduced data—before accounting for renovation costs or other expenses.

It's a shrinking cushion for investors who have long relied on a simple formula to fuel their business: Buy low, apply elbow grase, and sell high. But with elevated borrowing costs and renovation expenses eating into margins, there's much less room than there used to be for anything to go wrong.

The report, from real estate data analytics tech giant ATTOM, found that flipping returns have been declining for two years, with the typical gross return falling to 21.5%, from 27.6% a year earlier.

Industry observers note that "Flippers are still making money in most markets, but the typical return continues to narrow," Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM, mentioned via press release. "The second-quarter numbers continue the general downward trend in profit margins and gross profits we have seen over the past two years.".

So, why not skip the resale altogether and rent out the property instead?

After all, the promise of passive income—collecting rent every month while building equity—helped fuel a wave of small investors buying up homes earlier this decade when borrowing costs were low and rents were on a meteoric rise.

But the economics have changed for landlords, too.

Potential rental yields declined in more than half of U.S. counties with comparable data between 2025 and 2026, according to separate ATTOM research. That's to say nothing of the work involved in managing a rental property, which, as Realtor.com® previously reported, has proved to be anything but passive.

In a market defined by high carrying costs and shrinking returns, the better strategy may come down to which risks an investor can afford to weather—and for how long.

Despite shrinking profits, an index of fix-and-flip market conditions remained in expansion territory in the third quarter of 2026, according to a November survey of roughly 280 investors from John Burns Research and Consulting and Kiavi.

Some 66% of respondents reported selling most of their properties over the previous 12 months in line with their initial after-repair value (ARV) estimates—the amount a property is expected to fetch after renovations.

“Flipping can be profitable in a hot market with limited inventory, where homes sell promptly and buyers pay a premium for updated properties,” explains Realtor.com economist Jiayi Xu.

By purchasing below market value and making improvements that buyers look for, investors can boost the home's after-repair value and pocket the difference. In the right conditions, that means faster returns than holding the property long term.

And the slowdown may be creating opportunities to buy at a deeper discount.

Competition for fixer-uppers has eased in some markets, particularly Texas and Florida, where 44% and 37% of surveyed investors, respectively, reported less competition than usual, according to the November survey.

"Fewer bidders doesn't make every deal a good one," cautions Charles Goodwin, vice president of investor mortgage sales at Figure, Kiavi's parent firm. “What it does is give well-capitalized investors with a defined exit strategy more room to be patient and negotiate. That's where experienced operators tend to separate themselves.".

The trouble is, it's becoming harder to accurately predict what that exit will pay.

It has been revealed that four in 10 surveyed flippers reported closing sales at lower prices than a year earlier, according to the November John Burns–Kiavi survey. Meanwhile, 20% said most of their properties sold below their initial ARV estimates.

Among those who fell short of their targets, 84% stated they had overestimated the eventual sale price, while 57% reported underestimating their costs.

Goodwin warns against basing resale projections on comparable sales from a stronger market.

"If a deal only works with last spring's comps, it probably doesn't work," he says.

And even when investors get their resale estimates right, renovations can consume a substantial share of the proceeds.

The average renovation cost was approximately $72,000 per flipped home in the third quarter of 2026, down from $80,000 a year earlier. Yet renovations still consumed a larger share of the average sale price, rising from 16% to 17%, according to the survey.

Financing adds another layer of risk, particularly when a project takes longer than expected.

According to recent reports, the average effective interest rate reported by surveyed flippers who obtained newly introduced financing was 9.3% in the third quarter. At that rate, an investor carrying a hypothetical $320,000 interest-only loan would spend roughly $2,480 in interest for each additional month before selling.

Just one extra month would wipe out more than three times the $800 saved over a six-month hold by securing a loan at 9.3% rather than the previous year's 9.8% rate, according to the survey's calculations.

And even when a flip does succeed, Xu notes that taxes can reduce the final profit. Properties acquired primarily for resale as part of a flipping business generally generate ordinary income rather than qualifying for preferential long-term capital gains rates.

With strong headwinds to flipping a property, renting out a fixer-upper can offer a better risk exposure, especially for investors prepared to hold the property long term, according to Xu.

“If you prefer steady income, long-term wealth building, and lower risk, renting is generally the wiser choice,” she indicates.

Over time, owners may also benefit from property appreciation and tax deductions associated with operating a rental, making the rental path more attractive for those focused on building wealth.

And while asking rents were in decline for more than three years, the market is beginning to stabilize. The median asking rent rose 0.1% year over year to $1,692 in October 2026, its first annual increase since June 2023, according to the latest rental report from Realtor.com.

Of course, renting out a fixer upper isn't entirely without risk.

Potential gross rental yields for three-bedroom properties declined in 54.8% of U.S. counties with comparable data between 2025 and 2026, according to ATTOM's annual single-family rental report.

"Even though rents and wages are rising in many markets, record-high home prices are compressing yields," says Barber.

And those projected yields don't account for the ongoing costs of owning and maintaining the property.

Katie Lyon, a rental property owner and host of the Landlord Diaries podcast, previously told Realtor.com that even profitable long-term rentals can leave landlords with little room for unexpected expenses.

"If the water heater goes out, you're back three years of cash flow," she notes.

It has been revealed that A simple benchmark can help would-be investors gauge whether a rental deal makes sense. The “1% Rule" suggests that monthly gross rent should equal roughly 1% of the purchase price.

When it comes to fixer-uppers, seasoned investors rely on a similar guiding principle. The "70% Rule," advises paying no more than 70% of a property's after-repair value, minus estimated renovation costs.

Ignoring this benchmark can quickly erode profits, especially in today's market where flip margins are already thin, warns Ian Hart, a seasoned housing investor and founder of Barndominium.org.

And the latest returns suggest that buying at the lowest possible price isn't necessarily the answer.

Homes purchased for $100,000 to $200,000 generated a typical gross flipping return of 28% in the second quarter of 2026, according to ATTOM. By contrast, properties acquired for $50,000 or less generated a typical gross loss of $15,000 before renovation expenses.

The November John Burns–Kiavi survey offers another measure of how cautious investors have become: About two-thirds of respondents said they wouldn't pay more than 70% of a property's estimated ARV, while the average maximum was just 67%.

Sources indicate that perhaps most importantly, though, buyers should look for exit flexibility. The best fixer-upper deals are those that work in more than one scenario—whether as a flip in a hot resale market or a rental in an area with strong tenant demand.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#179358. Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer

Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life.
  • Most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time.
  • According to recent reports, among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life. The discovery, made by researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC), could help doctors identify families with a heightened genetic risk and detect cancer before it spreads.

Most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time. However, approximately 5% to 10% are associated with inherited mutations that can be passed from parents to their children, creating a cancer risk that may extend across generations.

According to recent reports, among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These inherited changes can substantially raise the likelihood of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. Testing for BRCA mutations has reshaped cancer prevention and treatment by allowing people with elevated risks to receive earlier screening and preventive care.

Sources indicate that now, a study published in Cancer Discovery points to another gene, CDK12, as a potentially key marker of inherited prostate cancer risk. After examining genetic information from more than 4,500 people with aggressive prostate cancer, the researchers discovered five unrelated men with inherited mutations in CDK12. Every one of these men developed metastatic prostate cancer between ages 44 and 62, meaning the cancer had spread beyond the prostate.

"What's striking is that every patient we identified with this inherited mutation had already developed metastatic disease by the time they were diagnosed," stated senior author Dr. Alexander Wyatt, associate professor of urologic sciences in the UBC faculty of medicine and UBC President's Excellence Chair in Precision Oncology. "The opportunity now is to identify these families earlier and give people the chance to benefit from enhanced screening, when there are still curative treatment options.".

A Hidden Genetic Cause of Aggressive Prostate Cancer.

The discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about CDK12. Scientists previously believed that harmful changes in this gene developed spontaneously inside cancer cells rather than being inherited from a parent.

According to recent reports, to investigate whether the inherited mutations were actually contributing to the disease, the team examined the patients' tumors for a distinctive pattern of genetic damage associated with loss of CDK12 function. This molecular fingerprint helped connect the inherited mutations to the development of their cancers.

"The tumors provided us with a genetic signature that pointed directly back to CDK12," said lead author Dr. Sofie Tolmeijer, a postdoctoral fellow in the Wyatt lab. "It gave us compelling evidence that these inherited mutations were playing a direct role in causing their cancer.".

The findings emerged from a broad international research effort involving UBC, BC Cancer, the Vancouver Coastal Health Research Institute, and the University of Washington, along with scientists at institutions in Australia, the Netherlands, Spain, and Belgium.

Despite the potentially serious consequences, inherited CDK12 mutations appear to be exceptionally uncommon. The researchers found them in approximately one out of every 1,000 people with aggressive prostate cancer. Even at that low frequency, they estimate that hundreds of families around the world could be affected.

Sources indicate that "While this mutation is extremely rare, the discovery could be lifesaving for the families who carry it," said Dr. Tolmeijer. "Finding one person with an inherited mutation gives us the opportunity to identify other family members at risk and help them take action before cancer develops or spreads.".

Genetic Testing Could Help Detect Prostate Cancer Earlier.

One of the most promising implications of the discovery is that doctors may not need to develop entirely fresh testing technology to put the findings into practice.

In a recent development, the researchers recommend including CDK12 in standard genetic testing panels used to assess hereditary prostate cancer risk. These panels examine multiple genes associated with inherited cancer susceptibility, helping identify individuals who may benefit from closer medical monitoring.

Sources indicate that importantly, the clinical technology required to detect CDK12 mutations already exists. That could make expanding genetic testing relatively straightforward, potentially reducing the time and expense needed to bring the discovery into routine patient care.

It has been revealed that "One of the most exciting aspects of this discovery is that we already have the technology needed to act on it," said Dr. Wyatt, who is also a senior research scientist at the Vancouver Prostate Centre and senior scientist at BC Cancer. "Adding CDK12 to existing genetic tests is relatively straightforward, which means this discovery could move from the research lab into clinical care much more promptly.".

Could the Same Mutation Increase Ovarian Cancer Risk?

The study also uncovered clues suggesting that inherited CDK12 mutations might be associated with ovarian cancer, although more research is needed to establish whether they increase the risk.

Several of the men with inherited CDK12 mutations had relatives with a history of ovarian cancer. The investigators also identified another person who had ovarian cancer and carried an inherited CDK12 mutation. Analysis of that person's tumor revealed the same characteristic genetic signature seen in the prostate cancer cases.

Together, these observations suggest that CDK12 could potentially play a role in hereditary cancer risk beyond the prostate. Further studies will be needed to determine how strongly the mutations are associated with ovarian cancer and whether they should influence screening recommendations.

Sources indicate that for families carrying these rare mutations, the potential benefits of identifying their genetic risk could be substantial. Earlier testing may give relatives the opportunity to receive closer surveillance and, if cancer develops, begin treatment before it reaches an advanced stage.

In a recent development, "With the right genetic testing and screening programs, we envision a future where no one who inherits one of these mutations dies from cancer," said Dr. Wyatt.

The research received funding from the Prostate Cancer Foundation, Terry Fox Research Institute, Canadian Cancer Society, Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Michael Smith Health Research BC, U.S. National Institutes of Health, BC Cancer Foundation, and other funding partners.

Breaking: Miren launches flexible application deployment platform built for the agentic era

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1184 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Miren Inc., an agentic infrastructure company, launched its platform today to make it easier for developers to deploy applications anywhere they need, without requiring them to become a solutions expert or set up and configure the application.
  • Artificial intelligence coding agents have changed the playing field for developers by making it easier than ever to build applications, but getting that software into deployment has remained a challenge.
  • “[Our platform] transforms a computer anywhere you want into a place for your application to live,” Chief Executive Evan Phoenix told SiliconANGLE in an interview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Miren Inc., an agentic infrastructure company, launched its platform today to make it easier for developers to deploy applications anywhere they need, without requiring them to become a solutions expert or set up and configure the application.

Artificial intelligence coding agents have changed the playing field for developers by making it easier than ever to build applications, but getting that software into deployment has remained a challenge. Configuration of resources, storage and the actual end maintenance of infrastructure that keeps everything running can be a burden that requires constant attention.

“[Our platform] transforms a computer anywhere you want into a place for your application to live,” Chief Executive Evan Phoenix told SiliconANGLE in an interview.

Sources indicate that miren gives developers a way to turn virtually any computer, from a virtual machine or bare-metal server to a local system, into a platform for running applications. Developers write their code locally, or have an AI coding agent generate it, and then hand it over to Miren, which handles building, running and much of the configuration necessary to deploy it. Once deployed, the application is accessible through a URL, without the developer having to set up and manage the underlying infrastructure individually.

The idea is to take much of the heavy lifting off the developer so they can do what they do best: designing, coding and strategizing.

According to recent reports, “I was always interested in this, like the application development is sort of like the final boss of someone’s great idea, right? They’re working on this great idea, and they’re like, ‘Oh, now I need to share it with somebody,'” Phoenix explained.

The deployment is easy. A developer logs into their virtual machine or bare-metal server and installs Miren server, which then acts like a technician on the other end, watching over maintenance and deployment. The developer can then code locally, sandbox and do all of their work on a laptop or local machine, and when they’re ready, deploy to production with a command.

Critically, all of a developer’s data and application resources exist and run on their chosen infrastructure, virtual machines and servers. Phoenix stressed that this provides customers the flexibility to run wherever they choose and however they like. One customer in particular wanted to run software inside a German sovereign cloud environment, something that could be difficult with traditional platform-as-a-service providers that restrict customers to their infrastructure. Miren lets the customer choose an appropriate environment while keeping the same development and deployment workflow.

“We’ve really attempted to have people be able to control where it runs, but still have the ease and the flexibility of it just running on the internet at the same time,” Phoenix mentioned.

Miren also provides a third service that complements the developer client and the server: Miren Cloud, which is optional for a standalone deployment. However, it becomes particularly useful when multiple developers need to work with the same infrastructure.

Sources indicate that “Miren is addressing one of the biggest challenges in modern application development: giving developers the flexibility to run applications anywhere without adding another layer of operational complexity,” said Paul Nashawaty, practice lead and principal analyst, application development at ECI Research. “As enterprises expand across hyperscalers, sovereign clouds and private infrastructure, managing distributed clusters becomes increasingly difficult.”.

Nashawaty cited ECI internal research, noting that 61% of developers cite tool fragmentation as the biggest barrier, making more unified approaches to application delivery and operations a top need.

Recent findings suggest that alongside the platform, Miren is also introducing Workbench, an AI-powered infrastructure operator built into Miren Cloud that can help developers manage and troubleshoot their applications. Unlike coding agents that primarily work with application code, Workbench has access to deployed clusters and specialized knowledge of Miren’s infrastructure. Developers can ask it to investigate performance problems, examine logs and analyze traffic without having to manually navigate the underlying systems.

“Think of it as a teammate, a sysadmin teammate,” Phoenix remarked.

Phoenix added that many customers were already bridging the gap between development and deployment using their own AI coding agents, allowing agents to generate application code, deploy it and then check results. With Workbench, they can extend this into the operational environment where the application runs in production, where the agentic operator can investigate problems and help navigate problems specific to the end infrastructure and relate them back to the coding agent.

It has been revealed that miren is also introducing paid support packages, giving customers a direct line to the company’s team, which has primarily provided community support until now. Phoenix said the company is expanding Miren Cloud with services that improve the reliability of customer-operated infrastructure, including automatic database backups.

Industry observers note that phoenix also sees an opportunity to turn customer support into a continuously improving layer of automation. Rather than having engineers repeatedly diagnose the same problems for different customers, Miren wants to feed the knowledge gained from individual support interactions back into its AI operators.

In theory, that would allow the platform to recognize and resolve familiar problems before other customers encounter them, shortening the cycle between discovering an issue and making its solution available across the platform. This follows a broader industry trend in which companies have begun building self-diagnosing, learning AI agents that improve themselves.

A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1160 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder.
  • Sources indicate that the condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening.
  • Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder. Now, researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have uncovered evidence that challenges 30 years of established thinking and could open the door to a upcoming treatment.

Sources indicate that the condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening. A fresh study published in Immunity identifies a previously underrecognized problem involving natural killer (NK) cells, immune cells that normally help the body eliminate infected cells.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur. The discovery also points to a possible treatment using existing medications called JAK inhibitors, which could be particularly valuable for patients who do not respond to current therapies.

Industry observers note that "This study has revealed a fresh target for this inflammatory disorder and sets the scene for future clinical studies to explore the use of JAK inhibitors or other drugs to neutralize interferon gamma in patients with MKD," says Professor Mike Rogers, Lab Head at Garvan and senior author of the study. "This could lead to a targeted treatment that hasn't been tried before.".

Why a Rare Immune Disease Causes Dangerous Inflammation.

Sources indicate that MKD is a lifelong condition known to affect hundreds of children and adults around the world, although researchers suspect that many people with the disorder have never been diagnosed. Patients experience recurring attacks of high fever, skin rashes, joint pain, and inflammation in the abdomen. The most serious episodes can cause potentially fatal complications.

For roughly three decades, research into the disease has largely centered on macrophages, immune cells that help coordinate the body's inflammatory defenses. Existing treatments are designed to block an inflammatory signal released by these cells. However, approximately half of patients do not respond adequately, leaving a major need for better treatment options.

To investigate what might be missing from the prevailing explanation, the Garvan team examined blood samples from people with MKD and studied preclinical models of the disorder.

Recent findings suggest that their experiments revealed a significant defect in natural killer cells, which play an important role in the body's early defenses against viral infections. In MKD, these cells fail to mature properly and struggle to perform one of their most important functions: destroying infected cells before an infection can spread.

Industry observers note that the consequences go beyond an impaired ability to fight infection. When natural killer cells cannot eliminate their targets, they release large amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, activating other parts of the immune system and potentially triggering widespread inflammation.

"We found that these immune cells are essentially misfiring," explains Professor Rogers. "NK cells are loaded with toxic ammunition, stored in granules that are released to kill infected cells. However, in MKD these toxic granules can't be released from NK cells and remain trapped inside. When an NK cell fails to kill its target, it compensates by shouting for help, pumping out large amounts of interferon gamma - a powerful inflammatory signal. This activates other immune cells and causes the dangerous fever and widespread inflammation seen in patients.".

Discovery Challenges 30 Years of Immune Disease Research.

The findings suggest that natural killer cell dysfunction, rather than macrophage activity alone, plays a central role in driving MKD.

Dr. Marcia Munoz, Group Leader in the Rogers Lab and lead researcher on the study, indicates the results represent a major change in how scientists understand the disease.

It has been revealed that "This really turns on its head 30 years of dogma about what was thought to be the underlying mechanism of disease. In MKD, the primary problem is in NK cells and not in macrophages, as previously believed," she states.

To investigate how this cellular defect contributes to the disorder, the Garvan researchers collaborated with Professor Mariapia Degli-Esposti and scientists at Monash University.

It has been revealed that using preclinical models, the team established a connection between malfunctioning natural killer cells and the severe symptoms associated with MKD. Their experiments showed that when the immune system cannot clear a viral infection, the resulting inflammatory response can cause extensive damage to organs.

These results help explain why a disorder involving defective immune defenses can also produce episodes of extreme inflammation.

Existing Drug Shows Promise for a Upcoming Treatment.

The discovery has already helped guide an experimental treatment approach for a severely affected infant.

Working with doctors at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, the researchers explored whether baricitinib could reduce the excessive inflammatory signaling associated with MKD.

Sources indicate that baricitinib belongs to a class of medications known as JAK inhibitors. These drugs interfere with signaling pathways used by the immune system, including those involved in responses to interferon gamma. The medication is already used to treat other immune-related conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and eczema.

Doctors added baricitinib to the infant's existing treatment regimen and subsequently observed an improvement in the child's condition. Inflammatory flare-ups became less frequent, and severe inflammation affecting the gastrointestinal tract began to heal.

Although the results from a single patient cannot establish whether the treatment will work more broadly, the improvement provides encouraging early evidence for a strategy that targets a different part of the inflammatory process.

The researchers believe their findings provide a foundation for future clinical studies investigating JAK inhibitors and other medications that block interferon gamma activity in patients with MKD, particularly those who have not benefited from standard treatments.

Discovery Could Help Explain Other Genetic Diseases.

The potential implications extend beyond MKD itself.

Researchers have introduced the term 'prenylopathies' to describe a family of genetic disorders involving the same metabolic pathway affected in MKD. Early findings suggest that these related diseases may share a similar underlying problem involving natural killer cells that fail to function properly and instead generate excessive inflammatory signals.

If further studies confirm this connection, scientists may be able to identify common disease mechanisms and develop more targeted approaches to diagnosis and treatment across multiple disorders.

"Confirming this link could help end the diagnostic odyssey many patients endure for years or even decades before receiving effective treatment," indicates Professor Rogers.

Professor Mike Rogers is a Conjoint Professor at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney. Dr. Marcia Munoz is a Conjoint Senior Lecturer at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney.

An opulent five-bedroom penthouse atop Palazzo Della Luna on Miami's Fisher Island, listed for an astonishing $85 million, has just surfed to the top spot on the Realtor.com® weekly list of the most expensive homes.

The sky-high estate was purchased by Kayak CEO Steve Hafner and his wife, Staci, for $40 million in 2021. Originally listed in March 2025 for $85 million, the opulent condo has returned to the market at the same price. The Hafners could more than double their money, if they get anything near their eye-watering asking price.

Spanning the entire 10th floor of the boutique waterfront building, the 10,194-square-foot residence has 15-foot ceilings, oversized windows, and floor-to-ceiling glass walls that open to bayfront terraces.

Sources indicate that the open floor blueprint features a water-facing living room, a billiard room, a built-in bar, and a modern kitchen. A private fitness center could be transformed into a sixth bedroom.

A 7,300-square-foot rooftop has a zero-edge heated pool, a hot tub, a summer kitchen, two wet bars, and multiple lounges for entertaining.

More spectacular mansions to make the week's most expensive homes list include Kylie Jenner's Holmby Hills concrete fortress, a recently remodeled Aspen, CO, mountain retreat, and a waterfront estate in the Hamptons.

Beachfront retreat: This five-bedroom estate, built in 1969, features 3,495 square feet of modernized living space on 55 feet of Pacific Ocean frontage.

According to recent reports, styled by interior designer Michael S. Smith, the coastal sanctuary has wood paneling, wide-plank floors, and expansive windows and disappearing glass walls. The chef's kitchen has professional-grade appliances, a waterfall breakfast bar, and a dining area that leads to an outdoor patio. A sculptural spiral staircase leads upstairs to the primary suite, which has a vaulted ceiling, a sitting area, and a private terrace.

There is also a three-car garage and a detached one-bedroom guesthouse.

Chris Cortazzo of Compass is the listing agent.

Concrete fortress: Kylie Jenner is once again looking to part ways with her Holmby Hills mansion, which she purchased for $36.5 million in 2020.

Recent findings suggest that the 15,227-square-foot estate first hit the market in 2025 for a $48 million, followed by several price cuts. Highlights of the seven-bedroom sanctuary, designed for "five-star resort-style living," include a primary wing with dual bathrooms, multiple fireplaces, a private den, and an outdoor lounge. Two guest suites have separate living areas, kitchenettes, and an expansive deck.

Industry observers note that outdoor entertaining areas include a geometric zero-edge pool, professional pickleball and basketball courts, a commercial-grade kitchen, and a private gym. The nearly 1-acre lot also has a guardhouse, a four-car garage, and five covered parking spaces.

Joshua Altman of Douglas Elliman of California Inc. is the listing agent.

The Gallery House: Built in 2006, this mountain retreat was recently remodeled and "exquisitely furnished" to offer a modern 7,870-square-foot interior.

According to recent reports, designed for entertaining, the elegant kitchen has dual convection ovens, two dishwashers, a wet bar, and a coffee bar. Each of the six en suite bedrooms has a patio or walkout access and features amenities such as a fireplace, a steam shower, and a soaking tub. Other highlights include a wine cellar, an executive office, a mudroom with ski lockers, a bunk room, a private gym, a massage room, and a primary suite with oxygen supplementation.

Located adjacent to the Tiehack Chairlift and minutes from downtown Aspen, the 1.15-acre property also has multiple outdoor entertaining areas, a hot tub, a cold plunge, a pizza oven, a wooden playset, and a four-car garage with a lift system.

Lex Tarumianz of Aspen Snowmass Sotheby's International Realty is the listing agent.

The Madison Club: This flagship sanctuary developed by Gala Asher might be the "final spec estate he will ever build in the community.".

The 14,000-square-foot open floor plan has six bedrooms, 10 bathrooms, a secondary professional chef's kitchen, and a "world-class" cinema. A lavish 3,000-square-foot primary "penthouse" has "explosive" mountain views. Other highlights include an expansive motor court, a seven-car garage, and a "rare" zero-edge circular pool and spa.

The 1-acre property also has a pickleball court and a fitness center that open to the pool deck.

Ginger Glass of Compass is the listing agent.

Waterfront Hamptons: The sellers bought this 2.63-acre property for $12.5 million in 2012 and built an 8,300-square-foot mansion in 2016.

The eight-bedroom shingled residence has sweeping views of the Atlantic Ocean and Shinnecock Bay. The timeless interior features custom millwork, built-in seating, four fireplaces, oversized windows, and French doors that open to covered porches. The grand kitchen has an island with dual sinks, a breakfast bar, and glass doors that lead to a water-facing deck. Two bunk rooms are ideal for hosting guests.

In a recent development, the property also has a tennis court and swimming pool. A wooden bridge leading to the beach provides direct access to the water.

Danielle Grossi of The Agency Hamptons is the listing agent.

Cocoloba: This 5.07-acre compound is said to be owned by Al-Fe Heat Treating founder Kurt Westman and his wife, Kathi, who purchased it for $3 million in 2011 and then built a tropical paradise in 2017.

Sources indicate that the 9,843-square-foot estate, tucked away on a private peninsula, features a six-bedroom primary residence and a detached guest residence connected by a walking bridge. Designed for grand-scale entertaining, the light-filled open floor plan includes a stunning two-story great room with floor-to-ceiling windows capturing the oceanfront views; a chef's kitchen with a butler's pantry, catering area, and wine room; and a sun-soaked primary suite with a sitting room, two vanities, dual water closets, a walk-in shower, and a soaking tub.

Garden pathways wind through the lushly landscaped lot, which also has a reflective saltwater pond, a heated swimming pool with a waterfall grotto, a private beach, and multiple waterfront entertainment spaces.

Offering direct access to the Atlantic Ocean, the property has approximately 450 feet of dockage extending into a protected basin, along with an air-conditioned boathouse, a tackle room, and a workshop.

Eric Rizzo of Ocean Sotheby's International Realty is the listing agent.

According to recent reports, the Atlantic Anchor: This seven-bedroom coastal retreat is remarked to be owned by real estate developer Daniel E. Edwards, who purchased the 1.02-acre property for $22 million in 2023.

Sources indicate that built in 2020 in the private enclave of Harbor Court, which comprises just two oceanfront estates, this 15,150-square-foot mansion has 150 feet of frontage along the Atlantic Ocean. The elegant interior features an elevator, a private office, a third-floor clubroom with a bar and home theater, a 500-bottle wine cellar, and a primary suite with dual spa-inspired bathrooms and a wraparound terrace with Atlantic-facing views. Covered patios overlook the resort-inspired free-form pool with waterfalls, a waterslide, and a spa.

A tennis court, a temperature-controlled garage with RV-height doors, a workshop, a professional-grade golf simulator, and a two-bedroom guesthouse with an elevator are also on the property.

The Matt and Nick Team of Serhant is the listing agent.

Carla House: This seven-bedroom Trousdale Estate, built in 2019 and designed by architect Noah Walker, was formerly owned by convicted real estate Ponzi schemer Robert Shapiro.

According to The Real Deal, a liquidation entity for Shapiro's Woodbridge Group of Companies sold the 20,541-square-foot mansion for $35 million in 2019 to the current owner.

In a recent development, the open floor initiative features retractable glass walls, custom millwork, wood ceilings, concrete accents, and two fireplaces. The show kitchen has dual marble islands, a wine cellar, and a secondary catering kitchen. The primary suite has a leather wall, a private lounge, a soaking tub, and dual closets. Other amenities include a home theater with stadium seating, a fitness studio, a wellness center, a home office, service quarters, and a roof deck.

The 1.14-acre lot also has an 80-foot pool and a four-car garage.

Tomer Fridman of The Beverly Hills Estates Inc. is the listing agent.

Bighorn Golf Club: This Guy Dreier–designed curvilinear estate, perched atop a summit on 7.64 acres, offers views spanning the Coachella Valley to the Santa Rosa Mountains.

According to recent reports, built in 2007 for publishing executive Duane Hagadone, the seven-bedroom "architectural masterpiece" is "organically sculpted" into desert bedrock with titanium, copper, and glass. It was last sold for $42 million in 2022, then hit the market in March 2025 for $59 million. It has now returned with a substantial price increase.

Industry observers note that eye-popping amenities include interlocking sculptural pools, three spas, an open-air glass elevator, a 10-car garage, a private view-top pickleball court, an aquatic walkway flanked by exotic marine life, and a detached four-suite guest wing. The primary wing has book-matched Golden onyx, a spa bath, a plunge pool, and a cantilevered cliffside office. A commercial kitchen was designed for entertaining. The home is being offered fully furnished.

A $1,812 monthly association fee provides access to championship golf, a 13,000-square-foot wellness center, and fine dining.

Ginger Glass of Compass is the listing agent.

Palazzo Della Luna: This full-floor penthouse owned by Kayak CEO Steve Hafner last changed hands for $40 million in 2021.

According to recent reports, spanning the entire 10th floor, the five-bedroom condo was designed to feature breathtaking views from nearly every room. Built in 2019, the 10,194-square-foot open floor initiative features 15-foot ceilings and floor-to-ceiling glass walls that capture vistas stretching from the Atlantic Ocean and Biscayne Bay to Government Cut, Fisher Island, and the Miami skyline.

It also has a private 7,322-square-foot rooftop terrace, along with nearly 2,000 square feet of covered wraparound terraces to soak in the ocean and city scenery.

Jill Eber of Coldwell Banker Realty is the listing agent.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 12:40 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Boston-based Aevius Labs Inc., a clinical medical data company, today announced it has raised $22 million in funding led by Insight Partners to build and train artificial intelligence foundation models that can understand and query unstructured medical text, imaging and other data.

A spinout of Mass General Brigham, a nonprofit academic healthcare system in Massachusetts, the company develops AI models that turn information from healthcare, payer, and life sciences organizations into insights other AI tools can act on. The company mentioned it wants to provide a foundational “brain” that can take notes, medical artifacts, clinicians’ transcriptions, lab work, radiology imaging, electronic health record information and other specialty medical data, and make it more accessible to healthcare workers.

Industry observers note that the platform can take all this information and use it to represent the whole patient, their medical experience, population studies and actionable insights for clinicians and doctors in the language that they speak. The organization noted it’s designed to support applications spanning healthcare delivery, operations, and life sciences.

The tech giant was founded by key members of Modella AI Inc., which was acquired by pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca PLC, using the company’s AI model and agent development for oncology research.

“Our mission is to make medicine computable,” noted co-founder and Chief Executive Rowland Pettit, M.D., Ph.D. “As a physician-scientist, I’ve worked across many types of clinical data, and there is far more knowledge in those records than we’re able to use today.”.

Sources indicate that the company said its models learn relationships across different forms of medical data and throughout a patient’s history. It does this by building a dynamic, refreshable representation of the patient, essentially a computable picture of the patient and their entire medical clinical state and trajectory that the doctor or clinician can interact with. An organization can use this to build tools to forecast outcomes, identify changes and monitor outcomes over time.

“Most AI agents today piece together their picture of a patient from text, one question at a time,” remarked co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Ming Yang “Max” Lu, Ph.D. “We’re building a native representation of each patient’s multimodal, longitudinal history that powers prediction and analysis across an entire population.”.

Aevius said the capital from the round would support continued research and development of its foundation models and expand the firm’s engineering, clinical and commercial teams.

The organization is bringing its technology to health systems at large. That means advancing clinical research and reach, anticipating patient needs, and informing care delivery and resource planning.

According to recent reports, on the insurance side, catching disease earlier means fewer visits to care providers through preventive care, because catching issues faster means stopping them before they become life-altering, expensive problems to manage. For life sciences, it will help deepen understanding of disease to inform clinical development by using long-term patient histories to study progression and treatment outcomes, identify candidate biomarkers and find patients for clinical studies.

“We’re bringing general medical intelligence to [the] data, so organizations can build on a deeper understanding for their patients,” added Lu.

Inside a Strategy To Convert Shipping Containers From the Border Wall Into Affordable Housing

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1111 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realtor

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Flying over the Arizona desert one day in 2023, Beau Phillips looked out his plane window and spotted thousands of shipping containers—remnants of a dismantled border wall—scattered across the arid landscape.
  • That chance glimpse sparked an idea: convert the abandoned steel boxes into hundreds of affordable housing units and build a whole latest community in the Tucson area for some of the 40,000 low-income residents waiting for housing assistance.
  • Recent findings suggest that "These were built to keep people out, and now we're welcoming people in," Phillips tells Realtor.com®.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Flying over the Arizona desert one day in 2023, Beau Phillips looked out his plane window and spotted thousands of shipping containers—remnants of a dismantled border wall—scattered across the arid landscape.

That chance glimpse sparked an idea: convert the abandoned steel boxes into hundreds of affordable housing units and build a whole latest community in the Tucson area for some of the 40,000 low-income residents waiting for housing assistance.

Recent findings suggest that "These were built to keep people out, and now we're welcoming people in," Phillips tells Realtor.com®. "There is a poetic justice there.".

Sources indicate that phillips, a semiretired MTV Networks and radio marketing executive, first encountered the containers in late 2022, when he took part in a demonstration protesting then-Arizona Gov. Doug Ducey's order to install a border barrier made up of more than 2,000 double-stacked steel shipping crates, topped with wire, near Yuma and in the Coronado National Forest.

After the Biden administration and environmental groups successfully sued, arguing that the 10-mile wall of containers was illegally placed on federal and tribal land, the state took the barrier apart in early 2023.

Some 2,200 steel boxes were left in the desert with no blueprint for their disposal, until Phillips saw them from a plane and pitched state officials on a newly introduced use for them.

To bring his vision to life, Phillips founded a nonprofit, Boxes of Hope, and teamed up with La Frontera AZ, a major affordable housing developer and behavioral health provider, to create a village made up of 350 to 450 shipping containers transformed into rental homes.

This project is aimed at singles, couples, veterans, seniors, and anyone priced out of Tucson’s rental market, where the median asking rent in October was $1,133, according to the latest data from Realtor.com.

"We're really opening it up wide to just whoever needs it, and we will make sure that the rent that is charged is affordable," states Phillips.

Sources indicate that the proposed 25- to 30-acre community will take shape in Southeast Tucson, within 2 miles of the containers' current resting place to minimize transport costs. The site also sits along a bus line and within a half-mile of shopping.

Phillips, who freely admits that he knows "nothing about swinging a hammer," tapped Tucson native Ryan Egan, a veteran container-conversion expert, to lead construction on the ambitious building project, which is at the moment in the fundraising stage.

It takes about $59,000 to turn a 4-ton crate into a comfortable 300-square-foot residence insulated against Arizona's brutal 115-degree summers.

"It's about half the price that the city of Tucson now pays for-profit builders to build affordable housing, so they're thrilled," notes Phillips.

Each unit will be air-conditioned, with a private bedroom and queen bed, full bathroom, kitchenette with a refrigerator and a two-burner stovetop, storage, new flooring, windows, and sliding glass doors.

According to recent reports, "It would be almost like someone who lives in an RV park," explains the Boxes of Hope founder and CEO. "You have your unit that you live in, and you connect to utilities on site.".

The exteriors will be sandblasted and decorated with colorful murals celebrating Tucson's culture.

Beyond providing a roof and four walls, Phillips and his project partner, La Frontera CEO Dan Ranieri, envision a holistic neighborhood complete with a park, laundry facilities, a community kitchen and dining hall, behavioral healthcare, transitional housing for the homeless, and on-site training in building trades like carpentry and plumbing,.

"It's really a 360-degree solution to get people not just a place to live, but a place where they can thrive," states Phillips.

Recent findings suggest that boxes of Hope already has backing from Sen. Mark Kelly's office, the Arizona Department of Housing, and Tucson city leadership. The nonprofit is at the moment meeting with potential donors and pursuing government and private housing grants to move the project from planning into construction.

To any locals harboring "not in my backyard" concerns about the future affordable rental community, Phillips stresses that his team aims to be good neighbors from the start.

In a recent development, "We're going to meet with neighborhood groups. We're going to explain our vision," he notes. " We want to listen to people, but we also want them to understand that we're trying to do something good here. We're trying to take lemons and turn them into lemonade.".

He points to La Frontera's track record of managing affordable housing, which includes the development of nearly a dozen low-income tax credit projects since 2008.

Boxes of Hope intends to unveil its full development plan and the village's exact location site in January 2027, after signing a letter of intent with the landowner.

"He loves the concept so much that he dropped his price in half and said, 'I want to help you,'" Phillips recalls.

Despite the project's ambitious scope, the construction timeline moves swiftly. Turning a raw container into a finished home takes about two weeks, and once production ramps up, Phillips expects the team to complete 12 to 15 conversions per month.

Site development is set to get underway in spring 2027, with the first tenants poised to move in by the second half of next year.

Beyond Tucson, Phillips believes that Boxes of Hope could serve as a blueprint for tackling America's broader housing affordability crisis.

Recent findings suggest that " Last year, 25 million shipping containers arrived in the U.S. along the West Coast and never left because America doesn't export anywhere near as much as we import," he says. "Most of them are still sitting all along the West Coast in Seattle and San Diego and San Francisco and Portland.".

That need for well-priced rental inventory is felt acutely nationwide. According to the latest Realtor.com monthly rental report, the median asking rent in October rose year over year for the first time since 2023, driven by a sharp decline in multifamily construction,.

However, Realtor.com senior economist Jiayi Xu points out that container conversions have inherent limitations.

"A container can be converted into a studio fairly easily, but it is hard to build larger units with multiple bedrooms that meet the needs of families," she claims.

AWS is making AI agents more decisive and secure with its latest Strands updates

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that amazon Web Services Inc.
  • Today, the cloud infrastructure giant unveiled a newly introduced family of open-weight “decision models” called Strands Decider v2, along with the debut of Box CLI, bringing native sandbox support for popular coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Kiro CLI.
  • In a recent development, AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025, and recently the project has emerged as the centerpiece of the firm’s agentic development strategy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 13:00 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Web Services Inc. is trying to tackle two major headaches for artificial intelligence agents developers with a major revision to Strands Agents, its open-source toolkit for building autonomous workers.

Today, the cloud infrastructure giant unveiled a newly introduced family of open-weight “decision models” called Strands Decider v2, along with the debut of Box CLI, bringing native sandbox support for popular coding agents such as Claude Code, Codex and Kiro CLI.

In a recent development, AWS introduced Strands Agents back in May 2025, and recently the project has emerged as the centerpiece of the firm’s agentic development strategy. Strands Agents is a software development kit that gives developers a flexible, model-driven foundation for connecting large language models to enterprise data and tools.

After introducing Strands Harness, which allows Strands agents to be deployed in any computing environment, in September, AWS followed up with Strands Decider one month later. Unlike regular LLMs that focus on text outputs, Strands Decider is a category of decision models designed to evaluate scenarios and assign probability scores to a predetermined list of choices. At the time, AWS stated decision models can help to improve the efficiency of AI agent workflows, such as routing support tickets or choosing which software tool to invoke to complete a given task.

In a recent development, with Strands Decider v2, AWS is adding five even more capable decision models to its lineup. The open-weight models are built on Google LLC’s Gemma 4 architecture and they’re available in various sizes, ranging from a lightweight edge version to a beefy 31 billion-parameter variant for complex decision-making. In a blog post, AWS explained that the fresh models provide greater accuracy across text, image and video tasks, and deliver more optimal confidence scores, so agents can better determine when it’s OK to take an action or escalate to a human decision-maker.

The Strands Decider v2 models have also been given the ability to process longer inputs, including multistep agent execution logs, so they can collaborate with other agents.

Industry observers note that so far, AWS has used the Strands Decider v2 agents only internally, but it has seen impressive results. For instance, its engineers were able to replace Claude Sonnet 4.6 with Strands Decider v2 on the company’s largest internal ticketing system, and in the process they were able to reduce its labelling costs by 98%.

In a recent development, they also cut ticket response times by 78%. But that’s not all they can do – in its experiments, AWS noted, the fresh decider models demonstrated an ability to steer robotic arms, evaluate other AI agents and route routine queries to cheaper models when a more computationally intensive frontier model might be overkill.

The Strands Decider v2 models are available to everyone now under an Apache 2.0 license and can be found on Hugging Face and also the Strands Decider repository on AWS.

Strands Decider is all about enhancing the speed and performance of agents while lowering costs. Meanwhile, Box CLI is all about securing them.

Sources indicate that in a second blog post, AWS explained that many developers have taken to running their coding agents in what’s known as “YOLO mode.” That’s where they disable permission and configuration prompts so that those agents can run terminal commands, edit files and call third-party tools as they see fit in order to complete a task. It’s named after the slang phrase “you only live once.”.

Agents running in YOLO mode execute much faster, but they do so at the sacrifice of human oversight. And that’s dangerous. An agent without any restrictions can accidentally delete files it really shouldn’t or leak sensitive keys, or it can be manipulated through a malicious prompt to do something else that’s extremely damaging.

According to recent reports, AWS’ solution to this is Strands Box, which is an open-source operating system sandbox that enforces strict security policies on every agent action. It launched last month, and with today’s update, it’s getting a latest Box CLI that adds support for coding agents including Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code, OpenAI Group PBC’s Codex and the company’s very own Kiro CLI.

Industry observers note that the idea is that developers can wrap their entire workflow within an isolated sandbox to prevent any accidents from occurring. Within the sandbox, the agents will be able to work without restrictions, meaning they won’t have to keep pausing to ask a human developer for permission to do something important.

Instead, the developer simply applies security policies to safeguard the agent’s actions. These policies govern which files, commands and network hosts an agent can access, AWS explained.

The agent’s credentials live outside the sandbox, with application programming interface keys and AWS tokens injected only when a policy-approved request leaves the sandboxed environment. That way, the agent itself never has access to those sensitive keys.

AWS noted developers also have the flexibility to switch between task-specific profiles, such as giving a coding agent access to a repository while restricting a troubleshooting agent to read-only diagnostic access.

Like the newly introduced decider models, Box CLI in Strands Box is being launched today. It’s a substantial step forward for autonomous agents, ensuring they can work without constant interruptions while remaining on a very short leash.

  • In a recent development, brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into fresh markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engel & Völkers announced an Aruba shop, Realty of America entered San Diego, and eXp Realty added a Tampa Bay brokerage and an Ohio team.

In a recent development, brokerage expansion stretched from the Caribbean to the West Coast in recent days, as firms moved into fresh markets and picked up agents and teams from other companies. Engel & Völkers is headed to Aruba, where it aims to open a shop in April 2027, and Realty of America reached California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 of her Team Z Realty agents in San Diego.

Industry observers note that eXp Realty picked up a Tampa Bay brokerage and a Cincinnati-area team that spent 20 years with REMAX. Baird & Warner brought on Oak Park, Illinois, boutique Beyond Properties, and Dane Briggs teamed up with Phil Sexton at HomeSmart’s NEXT team. IRES MLS welcomed back a former staffer to run operations, and Howard Hanna Portside added an agent in Massachusetts.

Engel & Völkers expanded into Aruba with license partners Zobaida Akkari and Richard Franken, Aruba-based entrepreneurs with backgrounds in real estate, luxury sales, hospitality and tourism. The shop is projected to open in April 2027 at L.G. Smith Blvd. 330 in Palm Beach and will serve clients across the island, according to the company.

“Aruba is a compelling addition to the network’s growing presence in the Caribbean,” Stuart Siegel, president and CEO of Engel & Völkers Americas, remarked in a statement.

Realty of America entered California with Zandra Ulloa and 12 Team Z Realty agent partners in San Diego. Ulloa has generated more than $4.2 billion in sales volume over her 13-year career, and Team Z peaked at 72 agents and $589 million in annual volume, according to the company. Agent-owned ROA, founded in September 2024, says it has more than 3,900 agents across 26 markets.

“People around me may see what I am giving up, but I see what I am making room for,” Ulloa said in a statement.

It has been revealed that rene Carpena and Dana Carpena moved Florida’s 1st Choice Realty, their independent Greater Tampa Bay brokerage, to eXp Realty, where it now operates as 1st Choice Collective. The group brings more than 70 agents and support staff and recorded more than 325 transactions and $60 million in sales volume in 2025, according to the organization.

In a recent development, jon Bowling also brought his 17-person team in Mason, Ohio, to eXp after 20 years with RE/MAX. eXp Realty is the core subsidiary of AGNT Inc.

Recent findings suggest that baird & Warner added Beyond Properties, a boutique brokerage in Oak Park, Illinois, whose dozen agents will operate as Beyond Properties Group. Owner and designated managing broker Erica Cuneen, who founded the firm almost 20 years ago, will co-lead the group with team leader Cynthia Howe Gajewski. The group joins Baird & Warner’s Oak Park office and keeps its Marion Street location.

“This partnership will allow me to simplify the operational side of the business and spend more time doing what I love, which is focusing on our agents and clients,” Cuneen said in a statement.

Dane Briggs, an Arizona real estate veteran, partnered with Phil Sexton, founder of HomeSmart’s NEXT team, in a leadership role focused on agent workflows and AI integrations. Briggs has worked as a designated broker and title executive, founded referral brokerage Roosted and led expansion initiatives at Homie. He has also served as an Inman Ambassador.

“Before long, we weren’t just talking about what Phil was building. We were talking about what we could build together,” Briggs said in a statement.

IRES MLS, which serves Northern Colorado and parts of the Front Range, rehired Samantha Ewing as director of operations. Ewing spent 13 years at IRES as a projects manager and quality assurance tester before leaving in 2018, and she has more than 20 years of experience in MLS operations and real estate technology.

“Having Samantha return to IRES is an exciting opportunity for our team and the local industry we serve,” CEO Julie Dahl said in a statement.

In a recent development, howard Hanna Portside Real Estate Group added Melissa Winter, an agent with nearly 15 years of experience who focuses on first-time homebuyers, to its Massachusetts team in Amesbury. Portside, which has more than 200 agents, entered a strategic partnership with Howard Hanna in 2026, according to the organization.

“What drew me to Portside was the energy, the people, and the opportunity for growth,” Winter stated in a statement.

#179344. CrowdStrike’s Zscaler deal is a $44B vote for platformization and a long-term threat to Palo Alto Networks

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2025 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Siliconangle ↗ Open Full Page

CrowdStrike’s Zscaler deal is a $44B vote for platformization and a long-term threat to Palo Alto Networks

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2025 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For decades, the security industry has told buyers to choose best-of-breed security products, leaving practitioners to stitch them together.
  • In a recent development, this has been perpetuated by the major analyst firms, which have a Wave for this product and a Magic Quadrant for that product.
  • has long articulated the value of security platformization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 16:11 EST / NOVEMBER 23 2026.

ANALYSIS by Zeus Kerravala.

For decades, the security industry has told buyers to choose best-of-breed security products, leaving practitioners to stitch them together.

In a recent development, this has been perpetuated by the major analyst firms, which have a Wave for this product and a Magic Quadrant for that product. The reality is that choosing best-of-breed everywhere has never led to best-in-class threat protection.

Palo Alto Networks Inc. has long articulated the value of security platformization. To be precise, Fortinet Inc. was the first vendor to advance the concept of a security platform, but no security provider has pushed the industry as hard as Palo Alto. Chief Executice Nikesh Arora has been vocal about platforms as the only way to truly protect the entire attack surface.

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc.’s agreement to acquire Zscaler Inc. for $43.9 billion strongly supports the thesis. SiliconANGLE has been covering the deal, so I won’t rehash the details. In short, the leader in endpoint security is buying the leader in cloud-delivered zero-trust access. The combined company is expected to start with more than $10 billion in annual recurring revenue, and the deal is expected to close between August 2027 and January 2028.

Industry observers note that over the long term, the combination poses a real threat to Palo Alto. In the short term, it is a strong co-sell opportunity for CrowdStrike and Zscaler, with significant integration work between the two.

Arora has long argued that customers want fewer vendors and integrated platforms. Getting there can be challenging, as security teams often operate with an “if it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” mentality. The mere thought of replacing a working product is enough to keep even the most seasoned security pros up at night. In February 2024, when he cut guidance to fund the platform push, Palo Alto’s stock fell 28% in a day. Since then, the stock has recovered nicely, validating his strategy, and its rival has now raised $44 billion to head down its own platform journey.

Industry observers note that in some ways, CrowdStrike and Zscaler were the strongest argument against platformization, though one could argue that each was its own smaller “platform,” depending on how you define it. Each led its category, and the two were close partners, with more than 2,000 shared customers and 16 product integrations. If best-of-breed products, tied together by integrations, could work anywhere, it was here. The two companies are now taking it a step further. “When you integrate as partners, there’s only so much you can do,” Zscaler founder and CEO Jay Chaudhry noted on the analyst call.

The “why now?” question is worth asking, as the coming together of these two companies has been rumored for some time. The answer is that agentic AI creates upcoming challenges and risks that are difficult to address through a partnership. An AI agent runs on a device and then crosses the network to access models, tools, and data, operating at machine speed around the clock. A vendor that sees only the device or only the network sees only half of what the agent does. CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz said adversaries are “exploiting the seams and the gaps between companies’ integrations.”.

In a recent development, I agree. Every seam between products is a place for an attacker to hide, and AI-driven attacks exploit those seams faster than security teams can close them. But a platform is more than one vendor and one contract. It means one dataset, one agent, and one policy engine, so a detection on a laptop triggers enforcement across the network without a person in the middle. If that’s the standard, CrowdStrike, while it presently describes itself as a platform, is not today.

With Zscaler, CrowdStrike is more than just a product to fill a gap. Zscaler is a best-in-class Secure Access Service Edge stack that protects half of the Fortune 500 and runs what it calls the world’s largest inline security cloud.

Sources indicate that it is also built for resilience, which matters more than ever. Last week, I wrote about six major outages over six days at organizations ranging from Microsoft to the Federal Aviation Administration. Zscaler sits between every user and every application, so if it fails, the business stops. That has forced the firm to engineer for failure.

Its Business Continuity Cloud provides each customer with a dedicated backup environment in third-party data centers, on separate networks and DNS, with software updates deliberately staggered so a bad release can’t affect both simultaneously. “No linkage — no network, no shared routers, no switches, no shared network operations,” Chaudhry told me in a previous conversation.

Recent findings suggest that of all companies, CrowdStrike should value that. In July 2024, a faulty Falcon patch affected an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices. The standard objection to platformization is concentration risk, and it intensifies when a single vendor controls both the endpoint agent and the path to every application. Zscaler’s continuity design is the best answer to that objection I’ve seen, and CrowdStrike should extend it across Falcon.

The near-term value is commercial. CrowdStrike indicates about 8,000 Zscaler customers don’t yet buy from it. Channel partners already sell both companies, and the two sales teams already work deals together.

It has been revealed that after the close, Zscaler will transition to Falcon Flex, CrowdStrike’s licensing model. “A Zscaler customer can add Falcon. A Falcon customer can add Zscaler. One contract, one platform,” Kurtz mentioned. CrowdStrike expects about $1 billion in annualized revenue synergies within 30 months of closing.

This target seems bullish but achievable, as it requires no code integration — only sales execution, which both companies are good at.

Sources indicate that today, the Falcon sensor and Zscaler’s client run as separate agents on separate clouds with different release schedules. Kurtz promised that it will collapse into one. “The brand promise, single agent, that’s not going to change,” he said. CrowdStrike’s next-generation sensor can already inspect and proxy network traffic, he added, which should make the job easier.

Kurtz was also candid about the effort: “Yes, there’s hard work to be done. There always is in an acquisition.” CrowdStrike gave no timeline. The engineering teams can’t combine until the deal closes, which is at least eight months away. CrowdStrike’s largest prior acquisition cost less than $1 billion. Folding Zscaler’s global security cloud into Falcon is far harder than anything it has attempted. Until that work is done, the platform exists on slides.

It has been revealed that that gap gives Palo Alto time to further its own platform. It closed its CyberArk acquisition in February, renamed the business Idira, and is already cross-selling it to its existing customers.

According to recent reports, the long term looks different. If CrowdStrike delivers a single agent and a single dataset, Palo Alto will face something it hasn’t had: a rival of similar scale with the leading endpoint product and the leading zero-trust cloud on one platform. Palo Alto is most exposed in SASE, where its Prisma SASE business has been chasing Zscaler.

CrowdStrike plus Zscaler make a formidable platform, but it still lacks a firewall. Zscaler is a cloud proxy, and many enterprises that use it still run firewalls in their data centers, campuses, and clouds. That is Palo Alto’s core area of strength.

It has been revealed that looking ahead, that should open the door to another acquisition. Check Point is the obvious choice, as it will struggle over the long term as a firewall pure-play in a market shifting to platforms, and it would give CrowdStrike a large installed base. If CrowdStrike wants a broader networking portfolio, Fortinet is the bigger swing, with switching, wireless and software-defined wide-area network alongside its firewalls. The two already partner on endpoint and firewall protection.

Either deal would add more integration work to Zscaler, so I wouldn’t expect either to happen soon. But a company that wants to displace Palo Alto can’t leave the firewall to someone else forever. I understand zero trust can replace a number of firewalls, particularly in branch offices, but firewalls are here to stay for the foreseeable future.

The deal also puts smaller security vendors in play. Netskope and Cato Networks are both independent SASE vendors competing against a bundle, and Oppenheimer has already named Netskope an attractive target.

According to recent reports, fortinet is an obvious acquirer, but the buyer pool extends beyond security companies. Hewlett Packard Enterprise Co., following its acquisition of Juniper Networks Inc., is embedding security across its network and may seek to bolster that portfolio. Dell Technologies Inc. lags in security, with a portfolio centered on data protection and resilience, and could benefit from an acquisition to close the gap.

Nothing changes today, and customers shouldn’t pause their projects. I’d use the waiting period to prepare in advance.

Industry observers note that buy what is integrated. Ask for the integration roadmap with dates for the single agent, the shared data set and unified policy. Until those ship, evaluate CrowdStrike and Zscaler as two products.

Use leverage. Palo Alto is trying to pry Zscaler accounts loose, and CrowdStrike and Zscaler want commitments before the close. As Sanchit Vir Gogia of Greyhound Research told CSO, “Consolidation is sold at the first signature and priced at the second.” Negotiate price caps for renewals now.

Sources indicate that get interoperability in writing. When asked about lock-in, Kurtz said, “We have and will continue to work well with all of the other technologies and ecosystem.” If you run Zscaler with another endpoint product or Falcon with another access provider, include that promise in your contract.

Make resilience a requirement. Ask CrowdStrike to commit to maintaining Zscaler’s Business Continuity Cloud and its staggered updates, and to apply the same discipline to a combined agent.

According to recent reports, this deal settles the argument over platformization. Who wins is still unclear. CrowdStrike has to do the integration work, and Palo Alto has the better part of a year to persuade customers not to wait. The great news for customers is that major moves like this create a wave of innovation. AI is changing security faster than ever before, and a CrowdStrike-vs.-Palo Alto battle is good for everyone.

Industry observers note that zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.
