#179205. 10 pharma deals worth $9.2 billion to $41 billion, and what each buyer got

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3467 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

10 pharma deals worth $9.2 billion to $41 billion, and what each buyer got

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3467 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From Sanofi's $41 billion Insmed deal to Merck's Cidara bet, 10 recent acquisitions show what drugmakers buy and what must go right.
  • According to recent reports, drugmakers are buying other companies again, and the largest of them are spending billions of dollars on a single purchase.
  • According to recent reports, many of these purchases are defensive.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From Sanofi's $41 billion Insmed deal to Merck's Cidara bet, 10 recent acquisitions show what drugmakers buy and what must go right.

According to recent reports, drugmakers are buying other companies again, and the largest of them are spending billions of dollars on a single purchase. Drug and biotech companies cut back on acquisitions to a low point in 2022, then bought at a surging pace in 2025 and faster still in 2026, according to CNBC. The buying goes far beyond a handful of famous names, because by early June 2026 companies had agreed to 201 biotech deals worth $106 billion worldwide. None of the purchases that follow is an isolated gamble. Together they show one industry moving in the same direction at the same time.

According to recent reports, many of these purchases are defensive. Every best-selling medicine eventually loses its patent protection, and a drugmaker that depends on one needs its next source of revenue in place before that drug's sales begin to fall. Much of what these companies are buying hasn't proven itself yet. Buyers are paying for experimental drugs and for analysts' sales forecasts far more often than for revenue a target already collects. A headline price in this wave therefore indicates little about what a manufacturer earns today. It says more about what its buyer expects the next decade to bring.

Reuters surveyed large drug and biotech takeovers since 2015, ranging from Sanofi's purchase of Insmed to Pfizer $PFE's bidding contest for Metsera. Several of them aren't for medicines at all. Merck $MRK KGaA is buying lab-supplies maker Bio-Techne $TECH, Boston Scientific $BSX is buying device maker Penumbra, and Abbott $ABT is buying cancer-test maker Exact Sciences. That spread highlights that the buying reaches past drug pipelines into the tools researchers use, the devices doctors use and the tests they order.

Sanofi is paying to stop depending on one medicine. The drugmaker agreed to pay about $41 billion in cash for Insmed, according to Reuters, and with it Sanofi gains a source of growth separate from its blockbuster, Dupixent. Insmed already sells two respiratory drugs, Brinsupri and Arikayce. Sanofi is buying medicines that patients already take, not candidates still in the lab. Dupixent is expected to lose its exclusivity in 2031–32, according to a Jefferies estimate reported by CNBC. What Sanofi bought is time, with a second business running before its main one starts to fade.

The price makes sense only if Insmed's drugs grow as large as analysts expect. Jefferies analysts forecast that Brinsupri will bring in $6.8 billion in revenue in 2035. Sanofi is paying now for sales that are still about a decade away. That forecast also has to hold up against competition in the respiratory field where Insmed works, and AstraZeneca $AZN is studying its own drug, tozorakimab, for the lung disease bronchiectasis. A purchase like this does not repair the research gaps that left Sanofi relying on Dupixent. "The deal does not fix Sanofi's R&D/pipeline questions, but it buys time," Jefferies analysts mentioned.

Not everyone sees the deal as a stopgap. Barclays analysts say the deal improves Sanofi's growth outlook and could make the organization a more attractive investment. Investors agreed when Sanofi confirmed that it had agreed to buy Insmed, and they sent its shares up 8% in Paris. Their support matters because the bet belongs to Belen Garijo, who had been Sanofi's CEO only since May when she committed the company to the 2026 deal.

Whether Garijo bought a fix or only a reprieve will become clear when Dupixent loses its protection and Brinsupri's sales either meet the forecast or fall short.

Vertex Pharmaceuticals $VRTX is paying the kind of sum a major drugmaker spends on a broad business, but it is getting a small and specialized one. Vertex agreed to pay about $10 billion for Crinetics Pharmaceuticals, a deal that adds treatments for rare hormone disorders to its range, according to Reuters. Crinetics' business centers on PALSONIFY, a drug for acromegaly in adults. Few Americans have the condition, and Vertex and Crinetics estimate that only 20,000 of them have been diagnosed with it. With a patient pool that small, Vertex is not paying for the revenue Crinetics earns today.

It has been revealed that what Vertex is paying for is a projection. The companies expect the merged business to bring in more than $5 billion a year at its peak, but they don't expect the purchase to lift Vertex's non-GAAP operating income until 2029. Until then, Vertex carries the cost of the deal before it adds to profit. If sales come in below that projection, Vertex will wait even longer for a return.

Recent findings suggest that vertex is not buying expertise in hormone disorders. It is betting that the expertise it already has will work in a newly introduced field. "We believe Vertex can build on the strong momentum of the PALSONIFY launch by applying our experience in commercializing medicines for rare genetic diseases," Reshma Kewalramani, Vertex's chief executive officer and president, noted, as reported by Vertex and Crinetics. Vertex's experience is in rare genetic diseases, while Crinetics works in rare hormone disorders, which is a neighboring field rather than familiar ground. For the deal to pay off, the young launch has to keep growing, and the forecast has to turn into real sales by the end of the decade.

Vertex bought a forecast in a neighboring field, and it pays only if Vertex's rare-disease playbook works there too.

It has been revealed that merck $MRK KGaA, a separate company from Merck & Co, isn't buying a medicine. It is buying the equipment other drugmakers use to discover and produce theirs. Merck KGaA is paying $11.3 billion for Bio-Techne $TECH to widen its life-science business through lab and bioprocessing equipment. The company is paying for the tools behind drug research and production, not for a product that needs a trial win. This is a move into a neighboring field. Merck KGaA will profit if drug developers keep spending heavily on research and manufacturing, whether or not any single molecule works.

Merck KGaA has grown through large acquisitions before. It bought Sigma-Aldrich in 2014, so a purchase on this scale is a familiar move for the manufacturer. The Bio-Techne deal also comes under fresh leadership. Kai Beckmann took over as chief executive from Belén Garijo in May, which puts a commitment of this size among the first decisions of his tenure.

With no clinical gamble involved, the risk lies in the price. Merck KGaA agreed to pay a 24% premium to Bio-Techne's Wednesday closing share price. The company chose to pay well above what investors valued Bio-Techne at just before the offer in order to win it. Merck KGaA is also spending more than it holds. The company has about 2.74 billion euros ($3.11 billion) in cash and equivalents, far short of what it agreed to pay for Bio-Techne. It is funding the purchase with a mix of cash and debt. For the purchase to pay off, drug developers must keep buying Bio-Techne's tools in enough volume to cover both the premium and the debt.

According to recent reports, merck KGaA isn't betting on which drug will win. It is betting that whoever wins will need its equipment, and it is taking on debt to make that bet.

It has been revealed that abbVie spent its money to go deeper into the field it already depends on. The company agreed to pay $10.9 billion for Apogee Therapeutics to strengthen its pipeline of immune-disease drug candidates, according to Reuters. Immunology is already a major business for AbbVie, which reports $9.165 billion in net revenue from its immunology portfolio in the third quarter of 2026 alone. The purchase concentrates AbbVie's bets in one field rather than spreading them across several. That makes the deal a wager on staying ahead in immunology, where the company has the most to lose if it runs short of new drugs.

AbbVie isn't buying time to replace a fading drug, because its immunology business is growing even as its old best-seller declines. AbbVie reports that its Humira sales were down 31.2% in the third quarter of 2026, while its immunology sales were up 16.3% over the same period. With the wider portfolio climbing despite Humira's slide, Apogee is not a rescue.

What AbbVie bought is a set of drug candidates whose value depends on results that haven't come in yet. One of them, APG273, is a candidate aimed at both IL-13 and TSLP that AbbVie reports it is developing for asthma. It sells nothing today, and its worth lies in what it might eventually do for patients. Robert A. Michael, AbbVie's chairman and chief executive officer, counted the Apogee purchase among the steps by which the company "enhanced our long-term growth potential," Michael said. He tied the deal to AbbVie's future growth rather than to its current sales. For the bet to pay off, Apogee's candidates have to succeed in trials and win approval, and only then can they keep AbbVie's immunology business growing beyond the medicines it sells today.

It has been revealed that GSK bought cancer drugs, but what it is really paying for is protection against its own patent calendar. The company agreed to pay $10.6 billion for Nuvalent's advanced-stage cancer drug candidates, according to Reuters. CNBC reports that GSK is counting on the purchase to lift its revenue growth starting in 2027, and that its leading HIV medicine will start losing market exclusivity in 2028. GSK wants to be selling the new medicines before that protection ends. That makes this a defensive purchase, with GSK buying its next source of income before the current one fades.

It has been revealed that that plan still depends on regulators. "The acquisition provides GSK with immediate new sales growth opportunities," Luke Miels, GSK's CEO, noted. Yet the FDA faced a Nov. 27 deadline to decide on neladalkib and had issued no decision when GSK signed. The growth Miels described becomes real only after regulators approve a drug they had not yet decided on. Until then, GSK owns a pending application, not a product it can sell.

Even if the FDA approves both drugs, GSK appears to have bought steady sales rather than a blockbuster. GSK could collect a combined $823 million from neladalkib and zidesamtinib in 2029 if both win approval, according to a January estimate from CGS International reported by CNBC. That return is modest next to the price, and Barclays analysts see a firm limit on how much the deal can deliver. GSK chose lower-risk drugs that could reach patients sooner over a shot at a giant. That choice makes sense for a firm that needs a revenue gap filled more than it needs a big win.

GSK also broke a limit it had set for itself. Miels had noted he would pursue deals of £2 billion to £4 billion, yet the Nuvalent purchase is the second-largest deal in GSK's history. A chief who promised modest purchases ended up making one of his firm's biggest bets. That suggests even cautious drugmakers may be spending past their own limits during this boom.

GSK bought time, but whether that time is worth the price depends on FDA rulings that had not arrived when it signed.

Industry observers note that boston Scientific $BSX is paying for medical devices that doctors already use, not for a drug that still has to prove itself. The firm agreed to pay $14.5 billion for Penumbra to build out its blood-vessel product line, according to Reuters. Penumbra makes thrombectomy and embolization devices, which are tools that pull clots out of blood vessels or deliberately block vessels off. The purchase is also a return to a field Boston Scientific once left: It sold its neurovascular business to Stryker $SYK in 2011, MedTech Dive reports, and buying a leader lets it come back near the front. "We've really been looking for a long time on how to become a scaled, market-leading neurovascular company, not one that's coming from a distance behind the pack and trying to roll up a bunch of companies," Boston Scientific CEO Mike Mahoney mentioned. Boston Scientific bought a upcoming field and, with it, time, skipping the years a slower build from behind would take.

No clinical trial decides this deal, but the deal has been unveiled and not yet completed. Boston Scientific has agreed to carry the risk that regulators block it. The company would owe Penumbra $900 million if regulatory approval fails while every other condition is met. Penumbra's own break-up fee is smaller, at $525 million.

Recent findings suggest that analysts see a sound fit between the two companies, but Boston Scientific is entering a crowded field. Needham analyst Mike Matson regards Boston Scientific as the most sensible buyer for Penumbra. Even if regulators approve the deal, Boston Scientific gains only the chance to compete in a market that Stifel analyst Rick Wise describes as growing fast and full of strong competitors.

Boston Scientific paid to stop trailing the pack, and now it has to outrun it.

Recent findings suggest that many of the biggest prices in this wave of deals pay for drugs that haven't yet proven themselves, but Abbott $ABT paid for a business that already sells. Abbott agreed to pay up to $23 billion for Exact Sciences, Reuters reports, and the tech giant it is buying already has sizable sales. Abbott and Exact Sciences project that Exact's 2025 revenue will top $3 billion, so Abbott is paying for current sales as well as a promise. The deal also gives Abbott a full lineup of cancer tests rather than one famous brand. Along with Cologuard, the best-known screening kit, Exact sells Oncotype DX and the newer Oncodetect and Cancerguard tests. Of the three things buyers in this wave are paying for, this is the clearest case of a foothold in a neighboring field, and Abbott collects that field's revenue from the day the deal closes.

It has been revealed that existing sales don't make this a safe purchase at this price, and Abbott is betting on how fast those sales keep climbing. Abbott and Exact Sciences say that Exact's organic sales are growing in the high teens and that Abbott is aiming at a $60 billion U.S. segment made up of tests that screen for cancer or help guide its treatment. Abbott paid for a business that is expanding swiftly on its own in a large field, not only for its current size. Selling more into that segment depends on the newer tests, not on Cologuard alone. Robert B. Ford $F, Abbott's chairman and chief executive officer, indicates Exact's strengths fit alongside what Abbott already does. The payoff therefore rests on combining the two businesses well, not on simply owning Exact's revenue.

For now, Abbott has agreed on a price but has not finished the purchase. The deal, struck in 2025, still needs approval from Exact's shareholders and from regulators before it can close. The first thing that has to go right is the closing itself. The second is turning Exact's newer tests into the next Cologuard.

Until both happen, Abbott's move into cancer testing remains a blueprint.

Sources indicate that merck $MRK paid for a promise, not for a business with sales. The company agreed to pay $9.2 billion for Cidara Therapeutics, according to Reuters, and what it gets is CD388, an experimental flu-prevention drug that Merck states is still in its Phase 3 ANCHOR study. Merck is paying for what the drug might do, not for anything it sells today.

It has been revealed that merck's own accounting treats the deal as an investment in research rather than as the purchase of a running business. Merck expects to account for the deal as an asset acquisition and to take a charge of approximately $9.0 billion to its 2026 research and development expense. On Merck's books, nearly the whole price counts as spending on research.

Merck is making a bet this large on a disease that causes a great many deaths worldwide, and CD388 is meant to prevent flu rather than treat it. An estimated 290,000 to 650,000 people worldwide die of flu every year, according to Merck. The manufacturer is aiming the drug first at adults and adolescents at higher risk of flu complications. Those are the patients for whom preventing flu matters most. If CD388 works, it would meet a need that returns every flu season. That market is the forecast Merck paid for, but it is not yet a fact.

Industry observers note that the cost of the bet doesn't end with the purchase price. Merck expects its earnings to come in approximately 30 cents a share lower in the deal's first 12 months, from the cost of advancing CD388 and of financing the purchase. Robert M. Davis, Merck's chairman and chief executive officer, mentioned the acquisition "exemplifies our business development strategy of investing where compelling science and value meet." The science he means has not yet passed its final test.

Until the Phase 3 trial succeeds, Merck owns a forecast, and it will see a return on the $9.2 billion only if CD388 wins approval and prevents flu in the patients it targets.

It has been revealed that pfizer $PFE chose to buy its way into weight-loss drugs rather than build a presence there on its own, and what it got for the money is a forecast. The $10 billion deal gives Pfizer an entry into the fast-growing market for weight-loss drugs, Reuters reports, but Metsera's drugs have yet to sell. Pfizer's former research and development chief, John LaMattina, believes the manufacturer must see Metsera's pipeline as central to where it goes next. The deal's terms also leave part of the price open. The $10 billion headline includes contingent payments, so the cash Pfizer is sure to hand over is lower.

A bidding war, more than a calm valuation, set the final price. Pfizer offered $7.3 billion in September and had to raise its offer to $10 billion while competing with Novo Nordisk for the firm. The contest ended after the U.S. Federal Trade Commission sent Novo and Metsera a letter about antitrust risk, and Metsera's board then sided with Pfizer. Novo's offer carried "unacceptably high legal and regulatory risks," Metsera said. Pfizer paid what it did as much because of the fight and the regulator's warning as because of what Metsera is worth.

According to recent reports, pfizer won't know for many years whether the price was worth paying. Courtney Breen, an analyst at Bernstein, puts the revenue Pfizer would need by 2040 at $11 billion if the purchase is to earn back its cost. David Risinger of Leerink Partners expects Metsera's drugs, taken together, to reach $5 billion in sales at their height. Both estimates describe a business that Metsera's drugs would have to build over the coming decade and beyond. Pfizer will learn whether its bet works only as those drugs reach patients and their sales grow.

Pfizer bought a place in the weight-loss race, not a lead in it.

Recent findings suggest that merck $MRK & Co is buying Verona Pharma to prepare for the day its best-selling drug loses protection. Merck agreed to pay about $10 billion for Verona to strengthen its respiratory lineup as Keytruda patents near expiry, according to Reuters. Key Keytruda patents begin expiring in 2028, and that leaves Merck only a few years to line up newly introduced revenue. Verona can't fill that gap alone, given that Merck took in nearly $30 billion in Keytruda revenue in 2024. The purchase gives Merck one piece of a replacement rather than the replacement itself, and the organization is buying time in installments.

Industry observers note that merck paid almost entirely for sales that don't exist yet. Verona sold just $42.3 million worth of its drug Ohtuvayre in 2024, a small sum next to a price of about $10 billion. What Merck bought is a forecast of what Ohtuvayre might become. For the deal to pay off, Ohtuvayre's sales have to grow very large, and they have to grow before Merck starts losing Keytruda revenue to patent expirations.

Sources indicate that merck's earlier purchases give some investors reason to trust this one. Merck bought Prometheus Biosciences in 2023. Its 2021 purchase of Acceleron Pharma brought it Winrevair. "Merck deal looks good at first glance. Given their home run with Prometheus and Winrevair, this (Ohtuvayre) looks like a potential complementary therapy," mentioned Kevin Gade, chief operating officer at Bahl & Gaynor. Gade's confidence rests on Merck's past deals rather than on anything Ohtuvayre has sold.

Merck's record earns it some trust, but the deal pays off only if Ohtuvayre grows into the forecast Merck paid for.

  • Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.
  • The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 7:00 amNovember 19, 2026 at 8:01 am.

Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

Industry observers note that for the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel.

It has been revealed that nuclear batteries have been in use for decades, primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers. But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles remarked.

Boles mentioned the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release. “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”.

Sources indicate that long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”.

It has been revealed that retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “crucial step toward undersea superiority.”.

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”.

According to recent reports, next year, Zeno Power prepares to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

In a recent development, the maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The manufacturer is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028. Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Recent findings suggest that since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medtronic $MDT reported second-quarter revenue of $9.364 billion on Tuesday, up 4.5% from a year earlier and 6.5% on an organic basis. Medtronic stock slid 2.5% to $98.20 ahead of the opening bell.

Revenue fell short of the $9.48 billion analysts expected, and the growth rate marked a slowdown from recent quarters, according to The Wall Street Journal. The company said revenue was about 50 basis points above the midpoint of its guidance.

Recent findings suggest that cardiovascular revenue rose 10.2% to $3.785 billion, or 10.4% on an organic basis, led by a high-teens increase in Electrophysiology Therapies. Cardiac Ablation Solutions grew 58%. Neuroscience revenue rose 5.1% to $2.705 billion, or 3.2% organic, with a low-single-digit decrease in Neuromodulation. Medical Surgical revenue rose 3.9% to $2.245 billion, or 4.4% organic.

In a recent development, non-GAAP diluted earnings per share were $1.34, down 1.4% from a year earlier. Analysts had estimated $1.33, according to The Wall Street Journal.

GAAP net income was $2.802 billion, or $2.20 per diluted share, compared with $1.374 billion, or $1.07 per share, a year earlier. The GAAP results include a $2 billion gain on the separation of Medtronic's diabetes business, MiniMed Group, which the manufacturer completed through an exchange offer on Oct. 15, 2026.

Medtronic reiterated its fiscal 2027 guidance of 7.25% to 7.75% organic revenue growth and non-GAAP diluted EPS of $5.94 to $6.00. The company stated it is maintaining those ranges while absorbing the impact of the diabetes separation.

"Our leading franchises are performing well, newer growth drivers are scaling, and we continue to invest organically and through disciplined M&A to add fresh technologies and expand our growth opportunities," Chairman and CEO Geoff Martha noted in a statement, according to The Wall Street Journal.

The quarter ended Oct. 30, 2026. Medtronic also stated it declared its intent to acquire Contego Medical in November and completed enrollment of the Sphere-360 U.S. pivotal trial.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, with the stock market posting a remarkable rebound in the past 24 hours, and the outlook relatively rosy heading into 2027, there’s little to tip the wings of investors right now.And yet, whispers of a dreaded recession are coming from figures that Wall Street cannot afford to ignore.Among those sounding the alarm is Bill Ackman, the hedge fund titan who leads Pershing Square. Ackman’s concerns lie with the Federal Reserve, and whether it will raise rates at its next meeting in the second week of December.

Ackman wrote on X that financial conditions have already tightened significantly courtesy of the bond market, making borrowing even more expensive for private businesses seeking to invest. Capital expenditure, in AI infrastructure in particular, has been a key driver for the U.S. and global economy for the past year.

“The Fed’s 2% inflation ambition is misguided. Geopolitical risk and the required investment in global military spending, deglobalization and tariffs, and the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set,” he mentioned earlier this week (ahead of Jensen Huang’s return to chipmaker Nvidia, which prompted a swift turnaround in stock market futures).

“3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world,” he remarked.

Industry observers note that ackman’s call to end the Fed’s 2% inflation target would have far-reaching implications, if implemented. For one, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh has made it clear he wants to give consumers and businesses a break from prices rising comfortably above the 2% benchmark. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics’ most recent data, inflation is 3.7% annually.

Economists could make a plethora of arguments as to why a 2% target was introduced and should stay in place, but chief among them would also likely be the Fed’s credibility. As Warsh learned this year, if markets perceive any weakness in the central bank’s commitment to the 2% target, they will raise their inflation expectations in the longer term. This summer, that meant bond prices rose—Ackman’s very concern.

It has been revealed that and yet, a realist might argue that macroeconomic conditions at present make it practically impossible for the Fed to bring inflation back to 2%—while also being mindful of the other side of its mandate: to maintain employment levels. Apollo’s chief economist, Torsten Slok, noted earlier this month that, according to its modeling,  the Fed would need to raise the base rate by approximately 275 basis points (from roughly 4% at present to 6.75% by the end of 2027) to bring CPI back to its 2% target.

“The Fed will put the U.S. and [the] world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%,” Ackman concluded.

Despite Ackman’s concern, the majority of interest traders are convinced the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will indeed raise the base rate at its next meeting.

On CME’s FedWatch, 97.5% of rate traders said they are expecting a 25bps-point increase to 4% to 4.25% at the December meeting.

Recent findings suggest that wall Street firms generally expect hikes in December and into early 2027. Deutsche Bank’s outlook for next year suggests hikes in December, January and March, of 25bps apiece. UBS’s base case is similar: a rate of 4.5% through to December 2027, and Goldman Sachs expects two more hikes through next year, with easing resuming by late 2027.

According to recent reports, “Some on the Fed seem to be moving toward advocating a recession in the non-oil economy (e.g. suggesting a restrictive policy may be desirable),” UBS economist Paul Donovan said in a note this morning. He has previously argued that Ackman might be right: “The Fed is still looking to raise rates—perhaps aggressively—with concerns about ‘“’broader’”’ inflation. These concerns focus on oil prices (which the Fed cannot influence) and perhaps AI-related demand (largely beyond the Fed’s reach),” he said earlier this week.

According to recent reports, “The only way to offset those would be to create near-recessionary conditions in the parts of the economy that respond to Fed action. A Fed-induced recession is not considered yet, but some members mentioned the possibility of a restrictive policy in the future.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.
  • Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with major financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 19, 2026 at 9:54 amNovember 19, 2026 at 10:10 am.

Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering, with major financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

Sources indicate that for Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all. At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion. With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.

Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.

But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning, co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.

A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old manufacturer was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50, valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95.

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei remarked Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.

“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he remarked.

In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the firm.”.

Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the tech giant to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.

It has been revealed that what’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI, and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.

OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.

Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will upgrade the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • Industry observers note that the most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • Recent findings suggest that on November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

Industry observers note that the most important words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

Recent findings suggest that on November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division stated it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It has been revealed that it also noted it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

Sources indicate that early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

The staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

According to recent reports, that phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

Recent findings suggest that this is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

It has been revealed that the second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to users.

According to recent reports, this prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself says the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the issues presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

In practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

According to recent reports, for a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

Sources indicate that the framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

Recent findings suggest that the two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

According to recent reports, that sequence matters. The interpretation says what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

The practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

According to recent reports, the harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

It has been revealed that for now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free 2027 report: 1 to 3 minute videos get 36% more engagement on YouTube, and videos with a voice beat music-only videos on Instagram, TikTok and YouTube.

UPCOMING YORK, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Opening a video with a question reduces audience engagement on all seven social networks measured, according to a new analysis of 1.2 million posts by Vista Social. The research, which used Vista Social's AI to label images and videos from more than 22,000 brand profiles, found that opening with a bold statement does better than a question hook on all seven networks.

The full research report is free to read at vistasocial.com/research/social-media-content-performance/.

The findings challenge several common assumptions about content length and format. While short-form video is often prioritized, YouTube videos between one and three minutes long got 36% more engagement than the same brand's other videos. Instagram videos under 15 seconds got 17% less. A human voice also made a clear difference: videos with someone speaking got 18% more engagement on YouTube and 14% more on TikTok than the same brand's videos without a voice, while videos with music only did 10 to 15% worse.

Every figure compares a brand's posts with its own other posts.

Sources indicate that "Most advice about what content works comes from a few viral examples or from what marketers say they do," remarked Vitaly Veksler, CEO of Vista Social. "Our AI looks at every image and video our customers upload, so we can measure what actually works across more than a million posts. The lesson is practical: let people talk, put the point in the first seconds, and save the call to action for the end.".

The analysis is part of Vista Social's 2027 research series, which also covers social media benchmarks by industry, the best times to post, how often brands should post and how agencies run social media, at https://vistasocial.com/research. Unlike surveys that rely on what marketers say they do, the research uses AI to label the creative features of each post and measures how each one relates to engagement. The data is anonymized and aggregated. No figure is published unless it rests on at least 50 brand profiles from at least 10 Vista Social accounts, and no customer or brand is named.

Charts and data from the report may be reused under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (CC BY 4.0) license, with credit to Vista Social and a link to the report. For custom data cuts or industry-specific results, contact the research team at [email protected].

Vista Social is the AI-first social media management platform for brands, agencies and multi-location businesses. Its AI assistant, Ask Vista, schedules and publishes posts, replies to comments and messages, builds reports and runs paid ads across every major network from a single conversation, and its AI agents take recurring social media work off a team's plate on a schedule, in Vista Social or in Slack and Microsoft Teams. Vista Social's AI analyzes every image and video a team uploads, from its opening hook to who is on camera, and the Vista Social MCP server lets teams run their social media from Claude, ChatGPT and the other AI tools they already use. Publishing, engagement, listening, review management and reporting live in one platform, with the governance larger teams need: approval workflows, custom roles and permissions, SSO, and SOC 2 Type II, GDPR and CCPA compliance. More than 30,000 brands and agencies run their social media on Vista Social. Learn more at https://vistasocial.com.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The price of XRP has continued to slump to deeper levels amid the prolonged market volatility. However, recent onchain data has shown an unexpected trend in exchange activity.

According to the latest data from crypto analytics platform Cryptoquant, XRP is currently facing a severe supply shortage on the world’s largest crypto exchange, Binance.

According to the data, XRP’s Supply Shortage Index on Binance has surged to 2.4 as of November 19 despite the asset’s extreme price weakness in recent days.

Notably, the data further shows that the metric has surpassed the previous reading of 2.09 recorded on July 6, marking a five-month high in XRP’s supply shortage index.

It is important to note that readings above +2 are a strong indication of severely tightened supply, which means that the amount of XRP available on the exchange has decreased significantly.

While negative readings often mean the opposite, this means that XRP has witnessed a sharp reversal from the supply level seen on September 27.

At the time, the index stood at -1.5 while XRP traded above $1.50, signaling an abundance of XRP on Binance. This means that more tokens were available for trading during the period, which potentially added to selling pressure.

While that is no longer the case, the latest data shows that the XRP supply index has jumped by 3.9 points in just 53 days, moving from supply abundance to severe supply tightness in just about two months.

This typically suggests that XRP is being aggressively moved out of exchanges despite its prolonged price weakness, potentially driving a rebound in the demand for XRP, which could eventually trigger a price recovery.

UPDATED 10:23 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Intelligent data infrastructure is becoming a priority as enterprises move artificial intelligence beyond isolated pilots and into production environments.

The shift places new demands on storage systems built to support traditional applications, especially as organizations introduce AI workloads across hybrid and multicloud environments. NetApp Inc. is responding with a strategy that emphasizes infrastructure modernization without requiring enterprises to abandon existing investments, according to George Kurian (pictured), chief executive officer of NetApp.

Recent findings suggest that “I think that the AI era requires organizations to be really good stewards of their data, because data is the foundation for knowledge and knowledge is the intellectual property,” he told theCUBE. “To have knowledge, you need really good intelligent data infrastructure that not only allows you to extract memory and context from your data, but also to keep it secure, well governed and a resource that you can trust.”.

It has been revealed that kurian spoke with theCUBE Research’s Christophe Bertrand and co-host Rebecca Knight during NetApp INSIGHT, in an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. The event’s coverage featured NetApp executives and technology partners discussing the evolving demands on enterprise data infrastructure and the challenges of bringing AI into production. (Disclosure below.).

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with George Kurian:.

Here are three insights you may have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of NetApp INSIGHT:.

In a recent development, enterprise AI workloads are exposing limitations in storage architectures designed for more predictable application demands. NetApp’s Novus architecture separates data and metadata management so each can scale independently. The company’s AI Data Engine is designed to discover, classify and prepare enterprise data for AI applications, according to Syam Nair, chief product officer of NetApp.

It has been revealed that “Performance and throughput of accessing the data, that’s a necessity for AI, but that won’t be sufficient for agents to actually act on the data,” he stated during the event. “If the data is not ready and it’s not protected, you get fast results. You get compromised results, but they may not be the ones you want.”.

Sources indicate that the demands of AI factories are also changing how storage resources must be managed. NetApp’s approach aims to support high-throughput AI pipelines without sacrificing the responsiveness other applications require, according to Arindam Banerjee, chief platform and technology officer of NetApp, who spoke alongside Jason Hardy, vice president of storage technology at Nvidia Corp.

Recent findings suggest that “What happens is [that] different types of workloads like transactional workloads for metadata and heavy sequential workloads for, say, checkpoints, happen at the same time,” Banerjee told theCUBE. “Previous architectures did one or the other very well. They never were able to combine it and do both at the same time.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video interview with Jason Hardy and Arindam Banerjee:.

Modernizing enterprise infrastructure often requires organizations to accommodate existing applications while introducing new AI capabilities. NetApp and Oracle Corp. are addressing that challenge through a co-engineered, fully managed storage service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

“When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

NetApp and Oracle Corp. are extending enterprise storage capabilities into the public cloud through a co-engineered, fully managed service that runs ONTAP natively within Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. The offering is designed to ease migration of existing ONTAP workloads without requiring application redesign, according to Konstantinos Papamiltiadis, senior vice president of partnerships at Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, a division of Oracle.

Industry observers note that “When I’m going into the OCI console, I have the option to use the ONTAP as a native service,” he told theCUBE. “For me, the most important thing that we managed to build is, from an operational perspective, we bring everything under one single interface that provides simplicity and consistency.”.

In a recent development, the integration challenge extends beyond cloud storage to the networking and compute resources that support AI workloads. NetApp and Cisco Systems Inc. are expanding their FlexPod infrastructure with validated designs intended to reduce deployment complexity. The partnership has served 10,000 customers over 16 years, according to James Cole, vice president of data center networking, business development, partnerships and go-to-market at Cisco, and Alvaro Celis, chief partner and ecosystem officer at NetApp.

“Twenty years ago, 10 years ago, you would’ve been designing your data structures and your applications around the infrastructure. Now we’ve turned that on its head,” Cole noted during the event. “You’re really designing the infrastructure around the movement of data. Who better to do that together than the person you trust with your data and the person you trust with your network?”.

According to recent reports, another partnership focuses on private AI deployment and measurable business outcomes. The NetApp AIPod Mini combines NetApp infrastructure with the Generate platform from Iterate Studio Inc., doing business as Iterate.ai, according to Brian Sathianathan, co-founder and chief technology officer of Iterate.ai. In one insurance deployment cited during the discussion, an agent reduced accident-report analysis from approximately eight hours to eight minutes.

It has been revealed that “AIPod Mini has attached connections to the NetApp storage, and it talks to NetApp using the ONTAP protocol that’s time-tested,” he stated during the event. “Then, on top of the AIPod Mini, we are running our Generate software. That software has a [large language model] embedded in it, so you can run all your AI queries locally and fully privately within your four walls.”.

Here’s theCUBE’s complete video discussion with Alvaro Celis and James Cole:.

Industry observers note that as enterprises introduce autonomous agents into infrastructure management, intelligent data infrastructure must accommodate increasingly complex operational demands. NetApp’s unified control plane, delivered through NetApp Console, is designed to reduce routine administrative work through policy-driven automation. In one keynote demonstration, agents responded to a nighttime performance anomaly, according to Sandeep Singh, senior vice president and general manager of enterprise storage at NetApp.

In a recent development, “Agents can, in real time, implement the necessary quality of service rules to ensure there’s compliance to the boundary conditions there,” he told theCUBE. “And that way, no human is woken up. The right outcome is achieved, and there’s no noisy neighbor effect. And there’s an audit trail presented to the humans for going and following up.”.

It has been revealed that automation, however, can’t resolve organizational questions about data ownership and responsibility. As enterprises extend intelligent data infrastructure across applications and environments, leadership must establish accountability for the information those systems rely on, according to Helen Yu, founder and chief executive officer of Tigon Advisory Corp., who appeared alongside Singh.

“It’s not a storage problem. It’s a leadership and accountability matter,” she noted during the event. “When teams don’t have access to … trusted data consistently, they actually stop making decisions. They start making workarounds.”.

Anthropic stock touched an intraday low of $80.01 on Tuesday, an 8.7% decline, which put it under its $83 IPO price in the fourth trading session since its Nasdaq $NDAQ debut. The stock was down 7% on Tuesday.

The stock had already traded under the IPO price before the opening bell, reaching a low of $81.28 in premarket trading. Nasdaq futures were down roughly 2% ahead of the open.

Anthropic closed Monday at $87.64, down 1.43%, as other AI stocks rallied after Nvidia $NVDA reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO. Nvidia stock jumped on the news. Huang had resigned from the chipmaker on Nov. 12.

Anthropic's underwriting banks have exercised the over-allotment option, according to Bloomberg. That means the banks have no way to prop up the stock should it slip beneath its offering price.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 19, 2026 at 10:07 amNovember 19, 2026 at 4:42 pm.

In a recent development, editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Andrew Redd‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.

The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid promptly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.

Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he noted.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.

Nate Bek, a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

In a recent development, “I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”.

Recent findings suggest that for Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.

“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he noted. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”.

Industry observers note that after graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.

That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd noted. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”.

Industry observers note that redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.

Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

According to recent reports, he wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

It has been revealed that redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”.

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”.

Sources indicate that in launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.

“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”.

The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion organization Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

Sources indicate that A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

According to recent reports, while the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The manufacturer landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

In a recent development, team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd stated he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.

Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

Recent findings suggest that the company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.

According to recent reports, “This was always the end goal,” Redd mentioned. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”.

Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the average price of gasoline in the U.S.
  • The average price for a gallon of regular unleaded was $3.64 on Monday.
  • In a recent development, “The scale of decline has been a little bit surprising,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the average price of gasoline in the U.S. has plunged nearly 90 cents a gallon in two months, down to its lowest level since the early days of the Iran war, coming just in time for Thanksgiving travel.

Context, of course, matters. The average price for a gallon of regular unleaded was $3.64 on Monday. Though that’s 57 cents higher than the price a year ago, according to AAA, it has come down precipitously of late. And it would only have to fall a bit further to $3.58 to hit where it stood on Thanksgiving Day 2022. Over the weekend, in some parts of the country, prices at the pump could be seen hovering at—or occasionally even below—the $3 mark, a huge psychological break for consumers who have suffered through years of rising prices.

In a recent development, “The scale of decline has been a little bit surprising,” said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy. “But given how things have developed, it’s not really a shock.”.

According to recent reports, so why have prices fallen so sharply since late September? It’s a combination of geopolitical factors in the Middle East, typical seasonal declines, and refinery operational issues. And, no, there wasn’t any conspiracy to keep prices higher ahead of the midterm elections. However, President Donald Trump’s actions are key contributors.

Here are the five main factors causing fuel prices—especially gasoline—to tumble:.

Despite some ongoing conflict, the combination of U.S. naval escorts, complicated oil tanker transfers, and pipeline bypass routes have allowed the Middle East to return to nearly 90% of its prewar oil exports, even though prices remain elevated from high tanker contracting and insurance costs. The rising levels of oil exports—despite depleted strategic oil reserves worldwide—have helped the global oil benchmark dip slightly below $90 per barrel as of Monday.

Sources indicate that prior to the elections, Trump openly said he was delaying any major ramp-up in attacks until after the midterms. That warning was keeping oil prices inflated as oil markets anticipated more disruptions to global oil flows in November. While risks remain and no peace deal seems on the near-term horizon, the lack of an escalation has helped prices fall. “The biggest thing now is this looming uncertainty over whether there will be something concrete and long-lasting,” De Haan told Fortune.

From a simple supply-and-demand standpoint, fuel prices typically peak in the summer during the busy driving season and bottom out in the winter, when more people are bundled up at home. Although there are brief travel spikes for Thanksgiving and Christmas, driving is typically muted near the end and beginning of each calendar year. Likewise, fuel is cheaper to manufacture during the colder months. Summer-grade gasoline is more expensive because of extra additives required to keep fuel components from evaporating in the heat. Winter-grade fuel is cheaper and less complex.

Globally, nearly 10% of refineries remain offline, largely in the Middle East and Russia, because of wars. But in the U.S., there also were supply disruptions at ExxonMobil’s Joliet and Phillips 66’s Wood River refineries in Illinois. Those temporary outages from weather challenges and mechanical failures caused additional price spikes throughout the Midwest. “The refining issues were boosting prices ahead of the election,” De Haan mentioned. “As these issues have been getting resolved, they’ve been pushing prices down, coupled with the seasonality, coupled with oil markets.” Outside of the Middle East and Russia, China also had mothballed some refineries during the Iran war. As China has depleted more of its own reserves, the country has of late ramped up its output, including its fuel exports, adding to global supplies.

Refining complexes aren’t built to operate like light switches for diesel or other petroleum products. When refineries are pushed to run at their maximum utilization levels for diesel, that also means increasing their volumes of gasoline. With diesel demand surging in the fall, the U.S refining industry is on overdrive and raking in record profits, often delaying planned maintenance work until next year. “Refineries are operating at their highest November rate since 1998,” De Haan noted. “This may be the highest utilization year for refineries ever. It’s going to be really close.”.

According to recent reports, fuel prices remain elevated, but there’s no hiding how far they’ve fallen. As such, nearly as many Americans as last year initiative to travel for Thanksgiving. AAA projects 72.9 million people will travel on the road this Thanksgiving, only a slight drop from 73.1 million last year.

GasBuddy’s survey data showed that almost two-thirds of Americans strategy to hit the road this week. Close to 20% of travelers said they will cut back on other holiday spending to cover the extra fuel costs.

If there are no more major energy disruptions in the Middle East, De Haan said, the national average for gasoline could bottom out as low as $3.35 per gallon over the next few weeks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Nikesh Parekh on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:41 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:41 pm.

Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide, laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically.

Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a substantial decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman unveiled the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept.

Industry observers note that microsoft claims the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.

Industry observers note that the offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in fresh hires.

Sources indicate that the worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the organization decide for you.

I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?

Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.

According to recent reports, there is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.

It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one manufacturer.

Recent findings suggest that hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.

It has been revealed that the jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.

Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual firm. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.

The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software manufacturer.

It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.

According to recent reports, software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.

It has been revealed that this cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the significant platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue swiftly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

Industry observers note that the bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

Industry observers note that one venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

There are three fundraising paths.

It has been revealed that 1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.

3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.

The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?

Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

According to recent reports, there are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise. Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.

On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.

Sources indicate that other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

In a recent development, whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a fresh role, a company of their own or a year with their family.
