📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Sources indicate that zetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no new mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

Governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

According to recent reports, if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's upcoming private AI app, ZetaLabs, introduces alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a upcoming whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

The snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

Industry observers note that two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

On Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the proposal, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain notes it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain says the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange users depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

According to recent reports, scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

Recent findings suggest that on the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain states it will announce any change to the process in advance.

Recent findings suggest that the vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

It has been revealed that if it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

Taken together, this looks more like a retirement plan for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.

Sources indicate that shibarium processed 546 transactions, according to Shibariumscan data, marking a slower period for the layer-2 network after activity spiked to a high of 6,370 on October 31, 2026. Transaction activity declined afterward, and the decline intensified amid the sell-off that hit the market in recent weeks.

The latest figures suggest that fewer transactions are taking place across Shibarium compared with periods of stronger activity. The key question now is whether Shibarium can regain momentum in the coming weeks.

Meanwhile, development continues behind the scenes for the Shiba Inu layer-2 network, as long-time Shiba Inu community member and developer Mazrael revealed a massive batch of contracts deployed on Puppynet, Shibarium's testnet.

But in the meantime, Shibarium’s fall to three-digit activity levels is a major slowdown that SHIB holders and ecosystem watchers will be watching closely.

Shiba Inu's on-chain holders increased as the number of wallets holding SHIB hit 1,700,930 on November 19, 2026.

According to the latest figures shared by Etherscan SHIB, an X account dedicated to providing updates on the SHIB ecosystem, the cryptocurrency added 236 new on-chain holders in a single day, taking its total past the 1.7 million milestone.

In a recent development, the month of November has also seen consistent growth, with SHIB adding 4,520 holders since the start of the month. The broader 2026 trend is even more pronounced, with the number of holders of the token increasing by 152,300 since the beginning of the year.

While Shiba Inu's latest milestone seems remarkable, Mazrael suggested that the Shib ecosystem, including Shibarium, might have more holders than indicated, with 1.4 million holders of Binance-pegged SHIB on the BNB Chain.

"Shibarium has more holders than those you listed, though. But yeah. Well, there are also 1.4 million holders of Binance-pegged SHIB on BNB. But that's not actually CCIP SHIB; it is a peg," Mazrael wrote.

OpenAI asked me to assess GPT-2 before its release. The stakes are even higher now

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1694 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In 2019, I was at an artificial intelligence workshop at a D.C.
  • Sources indicate that I followed up with OpenAI and raised the potential, following on the heels of the 2016 foreign election interference, that the technology could be used by nefarious actors for large-scale misinformation campaigns.
  • Recent findings suggest that in retrospect, I was primed to see those risks because I had encountered a similar dynamic in my military career.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In 2019, I was at an artificial intelligence workshop at a D.C. think tank when OpenAI gave a presentation about a new language model they were developing called GPT-2. The presentation was intended as a show-and-tell, but I I started thinking beyond the technology to its potential implications for political influence and national security.

Sources indicate that I followed up with OpenAI and raised the potential, following on the heels of the 2016 foreign election interference, that the technology could be used by nefarious actors for large-scale misinformation campaigns. OpenAI brought me on as an early academic collaborator to study whether a machine could write political content enough to fool the people it was aimed at, such as leaders or the public.

Recent findings suggest that in retrospect, I was primed to see those risks because I had encountered a similar dynamic in my military career. As an Air Force officer, I had seen how emerging technologies could take on lives of their own. The Predator drone had gone from a surveillance platform to an armed aircraft that became a hammer for the U.S. military that made everything look like a nail. Obama mentioned in reference to armed drones that it was “so easy to use them without thinking through all the ramifications.”.

I wondered whether AI-generated content might follow a similar trajectory, developed as a research experiment in advancing artificial intelligence’s ability to understand and generate human language, but ultimately being captured for misuses, perhaps political manipulation or misinformation at scale.

Working with a colleague at OpenAI and another who would later join Anthropic, we researched that possibility and found, well before anyone knew about ChatGPT, that the technology could produce “news” indistinguishable from human-written content.

OpenAI’s staged release is the closest thing I have seen to what I argue for here: a lab asking people who study political consequences before it ships. The goal was not to stop development but to bring a different type of expertise into decisions about technology evaluation and anticipate its consequences. Some of the threats turned out differently than we anticipated. For example, the bigger risk now is not that people are necessarily fooled by AI content but that the proliferation of AI content means that people are more skeptical of everything they encounter. Nonetheless, the initial studies were not misguided and augured goalposts into place by which future evidence could be assessed, its own form of progress and preparedness.

The developers are certainly doing robust recruitment of economists, philosophers, and political scientists to study technological consequences in-house. But the companies still seem to look outward to “pace the frontier” when they are simultaneously at the vanguard of acceleration, one driven by enormous financial investments and stakes.

Indeed, AI development has raised the stakes of an old paradox: the people who build a technology are not necessarily the people best equipped to judge its consequences. AI companies are developing tools that are technically impressive, but are shaping everything from warfare to the global balance of power.

In a recent development, that some of the people building these systems assign a greater than 10 percent probability to existential annihilation—a number of uncertain provenance and questionable methodological foundation—raises the question of whether the capacity to develop sophisticated algorithms confers any particular expertise in assessing political or societal risks, let alone determining how much or what type of risk society should tolerate. The latter is a question of political judgment, rather than technological ingenuity.

The tension between scientific brilliance and political judgment is not a new problem.

Industry observers note that at the 1954 security hearings on Robert Oppenheimer, Norris Bradbury, the physicist who succeeded him as director of Los Alamos, described the scientist’s “curiosity about facts, about systems, about life” and a “willingness to examine, to be convinced and without a priori convictions as to the rightness or wrongness.” Bradbury reveals a good deal about what motivates scientists but also intimates the blindspots, a paradox about some of the most accomplished innovators. They are capable of extraordinary technological breakthroughs but, in part perhaps because they do not have those a priori convictions, are not prepared for the political consequences, while also manifesting considerable confidence about those same consequences.

Sources indicate that for example, Albert Einstein, whose scientific work helped lay the foundations for atomic weapons and who had urged President Roosevelt to support research that ultimately led to the Manhattan Project, believed that the nuclear age demanded a fundamental rethinking of national sovereignty. In a 1947 meeting with a U.S. government representative, Einstein argued that preventing atomic war required establishing a supranational world government to which nations would transfer their military power. The official who met with him was struck by the contrast between Einstein’s scientific genius and his political judgment, observing that international politics was “clearly not his métier.”.

The episode foreshadowed Mark Zuckerberg decades later. He had envisioned Facebook as a vehicle for global connective tissue, but the same technology that connected people also enabled political polarization, mental health problems for teens, and the coordination of political violence. In 2017, he wrote a manifesto that promulgated a 21st century version of world government whose goal entailed “establishing a fresh process for citizens worldwide to participate in collective decision-making,” using the tech giant’s technology of course.

For Elon Musk, the innovation was a Starlink satellite network that completely revolutionized communications and became indispensable for Ukraine’s war against Russia. But in 2022, Musk declined a Ukrainian request to use Starlink for attacks on Russia’s Black Sea Fleet, concerned about escalation. That the genius of satellites might carry over to geopolitics was an act of supreme confidence.

The common thread is not that these innovators necessarily made the wrong political decisions, but that their technological accomplishments gave them an outsized role in making decisions for which technical expertise offered no particular preparation. Qualities that would allow someone to make discoveries on the photoelectric effect that earn someone a Nobel Prize in physics are not necessarily the same as those dealing with social institutions and political interest.

Recent findings suggest that now, more than 100 years after Einstein’s Nobel-winning discoveries, the question of whether aptitude in one domain should provide legitimacy in another has become more urgent in an era of artificial intelligence. In the modern instance, a small group of technology leaders and companies are both building latest technologies and making political judgments about risks. What do the earlier innovators say about the limits of technological expertise?

Industry observers note that my recent book, Harnessing Disruption, reveals two patterns of technological innovation. One is that technological expertise does not translate into political judgment. The second is that even being able to anticipate political consequences does not fully equip them to control the technology.

Congress is now trying to force the problem: House Democratic committee leaders have asked five leading AI companies to report model misalignment incidents to Congress within 48 hours of detection, with a full accounting due Nov. 11. So far, the companies have demurred, and not surprisingly. At this point, the letters are functioning more as performative politics than a mobilized attempt to require disclosure. Lacking the votes and a developed legislative alternative, these members can try to nudge action but falls far short of Senator Dianne Feinstein’s admonition to Meta in 2017, “you bear this responsibility. You created these platforms, and now they’re being misused. And you have to be the ones who do something about it — or we will” that I argue in my book forced Meta’s hands on social media reform measures.

Industry observers note that another lesson comes from the first. Instead of reacting to political capture, innovators need to design these inevitabilities into the initial concept. In the Air Force, acquisitions officers such as myself were told to design-in notable features early, which meant working with operators, policymakers, and lawyers to ensure that we were designing something that could not just fly but be politically and operationally usable. In 1999, E-3 AWACS operators I worked with were telling stories about buying GPS receivers at Radio Shack because the military-issued equipment was bulky and cumbersome. Those receivers did not meet every military specification but were far easier to use, an example that stays with me as an illustration of what happens when engineers design systems that look good on paper but without talking to the people who actually use them downstream.

The same idea applies to latest technologies. OpenAI’s staged release was a version of it. An engineer at a blockchain technology tech giant whom I interviewed for my recent book explained why they didn’t invest in policy expertise early on. The competition to develop the technology was intense and if they didn’t build it first, someone else would. They could worry about the policy implications later. But a modest investment in understanding the political environment, drawing on historians, political scientists, and game theorists, might avoid far greater costs down the road.

The goal is not to restrain genius as a matter of principle, but to recognize its limits and broaden the aperture. AI companies have increasingly embraced red teaming that subjects models to adversarial testing and commendably publishing results, which is certainly more self-aware than the largely reactive experience of social media platforms, but they need to do more to look further down the game tree not just to see what the models can do but what the deployment might set in motion as second or third order effects. But those questions are difficult to answer when those asking the questions are also under pressure to ship the next model, and some of the third-party audits can face similar pressure if their access or funding hinge on the success of the company they’re examining.

As Peter Drucker, who spent decades studying the intersection of politics, economics, and organizational behavior, wrote, “the most serious mistakes are not being made as a result of wrong answers. The truly dangerous thing is asking the wrong questions.”.

Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors.
  • The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 19, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 12:51 pm.

Amazon and Latest York City are fighting again.

In a recent development, the Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518, would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.

Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing Latest York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported. Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post, Amazon stated it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the manufacturer wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in Latest York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”.

Recent findings suggest that amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel noted the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the organization works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

In a recent development, “We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel remarked. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The manufacturer also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

In a recent development, the standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled prepares to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

It has been revealed that amazon stuck with its prepares for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time revealed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise Upcoming Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections.We are crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.If… https://t.co/UWXVTJhRL6.

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” remarked Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”.

City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X.

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”.

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported.

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Recent findings suggest that amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The organization said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC. The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

NEAR Protocol (NEAR) fell 11.41% on Nov. 20 and traded at $2.84, according to TradingView data. In early October, the token was trading near $6, and it has lost about half of its value since then.

Sources indicate that over the same period, the volume of NEAR Intents went up. "NEAR went from $6 to $3 in about a month. funny thing is, NEAR Intents is doing more volume now than it did in october," NEAR ecosystem contributor Evgeny Haenko wrote on X on Nov. 20.

According to Haenko, NEAR Intents averaged around $129 million in daily volume in October, and in November it was processing around $134 million a day. "The price got cut in half, the business didn't slow down at all. hard for me to be bearish here," he wrote.

NEAR Intents lets consumers swap assets across more than 30 blockchains, including Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana and XRP. The service is built into wallets such as Ledger, Trust Wallet and Brave. Over the past year, its trading volume grew 7.1 times to $39.5 billion.

NEAR Intents has collected about $63 million in fees in total, and the network keeps about 29% of that amount. Fees on the NEAR Intents interface, payments from B2B partners and the spread on better-than-market trades accounted for 16.3%, 9.9% and 2.8% of the fees, respectively. Over the last 30 days, the protocol earned about $1.8 million, compared with $2.2 million in October.

Since February 2026, the protocol has used NEAR Intents revenue to buy NEAR on the market. More than 1.84 million NEAR have gone to the buyback wallet so far, and that is 41.6% of all distributed onchain revenue. Base transaction fees on the network are burned in full.

In early November, the NEAR community also voted to cut the maximum annual issuance from 2.5% to 1.6% over two years. The proposal, HSP-029, went through House of Stake, NEAR's governance initiative, and Haenko is one of its participants.

On Sept. 29, Bitwise launched the first U.S. spot NEAR ETF on NYSE Arca under the ticker NRR. Two days later, on Oct. 1, NEAR Intents paused its services after an exploit that cost about $3.8 million, and the team promised to compensate consumers in full. The exploiter later returned the funds. "The funds from the $3.8M NEAR Intents hack were sent back in full," NEAR Intents general manager Alex Shevchenko said at the time.

#179178. Tech Report: Opdivo, Jardiance and Xtandi: 3 drugs facing copies on different clocks

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1163 w)

Tech Report: Opdivo, Jardiance and Xtandi: 3 drugs facing copies on different clocks

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1163 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, patent expiry dates rarely mark when sales fall.
  • A patent lets a drugmaker sell a best-selling medicine without competition from cheaper copies, and for several of the industry's biggest products, that protection is running out at about the same time.
  • In a recent development, it matters because drugmakers use revenue from today's best-sellers to fund the research behind tomorrow's.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, patent expiry dates rarely mark when sales fall. 3 blockbuster drugs, Opdivo, Jardiance and Xtandi, show how copies arrive.

A patent lets a drugmaker sell a best-selling medicine without competition from cheaper copies, and for several of the industry's biggest products, that protection is running out at about the same time. The 20 largest biopharma companies stood to lose $180 billion in revenue to expiring patents through 2028, according to a 2024 EY estimate reported by CNBC. That covers only the biggest companies and only a few years, and it's still a number every major drugmaker has to plan around.

In a recent development, it matters because drugmakers use revenue from today's best-sellers to fund the research behind tomorrow's. So for investors, patients and the companies themselves, the real question is how fast that money disappears once protection ends.

Drugmakers aren't sitting still. They tweak their drugs and fight to defend their exclusivity, pushing the loss further out. But they can only delay it, not stop it. "While you can tack on some years and extend revenues, there's only so much time you can add," Mike Perrone, a biotech specialist at Baird, told CNBC in 2024. Those extra years buy time to launch fresh products, not a permanent escape.

The losses also don't arrive all at once. Copies can hit one country before another, and the type of drug affects how quickly rivals can win patients over. That's why a patent's expiration date is a poor guide to when a blockbuster's sales will actually fall.

In a recent development, the Wall Street Journal identified the top-selling drugs about to lose patent protection, from Astellas' Xtandi to Bristol Myers Squibb's cancer drug Opdivo. They don't share a single deadline. Each faces its own fight over how long sales hold up, in courts, before regulators, in pharmacies and country by country. For each one, the question is what decides how fast sales fall.

Bristol Myers Squibb will lose patent protection on its cancer immunotherapy Opdivo this decade, The Wall Street Journal reports, with the drug's key patent expiring in 2028, according to CNBC. A lot is riding on it: Opdivo brought in $8.25 billion in 2022. With that much revenue at risk so soon, the question isn't whether Bristol Myers loses Opdivo's sales, but how fast.

According to recent reports, that depends on what kind of drug Opdivo is. It's a biologic, and copies of biologics, known as biosimilars, have been slow to steal business from the originals. AbbVie lost only a small share of the market for Humira after biosimilars launched in 2023, according to Bioepis figures reported by CNBC, and biosimilars overall were still slow to catch on in 2024, William Blair analyst Matt Phipps told CNBC. That's no forecast for Opdivo, but it suggests Bristol Myers is unlikely to lose most of the drug's revenue the year its patent expires.

Sources indicate that A slower decline still ends with a much smaller drug, though. Opdivo could bring in $3.18 billion in 2032, according to a 2024 Leerink Partners estimate reported by CNBC, far less than its 2022 sales. Being a biologic buys Bristol Myers time, not protection.

Industry observers note that boehringer Ingelheim's diabetes drug Jardiance is one of the industry's biggest sellers headed toward the end of patent protection, according to The Wall Street Journal. The patent on its active ingredient, empagliflozin, runs until November 2029, according to The Pharma Letter. That gives Boehringer time to line up replacements, assuming rivals wait for the patent to expire before selling copies. In Russia, one hasn't.

It has been revealed that russian drugmaker Grotex has launched its own generic version of Jardiance, according to The Pharma Letter, and Boehringer states it infringes the patent. No ruling has been reported, so for now that's an accusation, not a proven violation. But the dispute was public by early September 2026, years before the patent runs out, which means Boehringer may already be losing Jardiance sales in one country.

Sources indicate that its other big drug, the blood thinner Eliquis, is under pressure too. Eliquis makes up 30% of the company's revenue, according to The Wall Street Journal, and it was among the first 10 drugs picked for Medicare price negotiations. The negotiated price took effect in January 2026, two years before Opdivo's key patent expires.

To fill the gap, Bristol Myers is buying new products, including through its acquisition of Karuna Therapeutics. JPMorgan analyst Chris Schott told CNBC in 2024 that he expected those products to "ultimately position the firm for growth." But that growth would come only after much of Opdivo's revenue is already gone.

Bristol Myers has a few years to prove its new drugs can replace an old one that copies will slowly eat away.

Boehringer is treating the copy as a fair-competition issue as well as a patent fight. It has brought in Russia's antitrust regulator, the Federal Anti-Monopoly Service, giving it a second way to press its case.

Jardiance faces pressure in the U.S., too. Like Eliquis, it was one of the first 10 drugs picked for Medicare price negotiations, and its negotiated price took effect in January 2026. Boehringer is defending Jardiance one country at a time, and it can't count on untouched sales until the patent expires in 2029.

Recent findings suggest that for most blockbusters on this list, losing patent protection is still a future worry. For Astellas' prostate cancer drug Xtandi, it's already started. Xtandi's compound patent in South Korea expired on June 27, 2026, according to Dailypharm, and generic copies hit the market the next day. That date applies only to South Korea, so it isn't the moment Astellas loses exclusivity everywhere. But it offers an early look at how generic makers move in and how a brand fights back.

On paper, Astellas had a backup. A second patent, covering how the drug is formulated, runs until September 2033. But Korean drugmakers including GL Pharma, Hanmi, Chong Kun Dang, JW Pharmaceutical and Alvogen Korea won rulings that let their versions get around it. The backup bought Astellas no extra time, a reminder that the secondary patents a brand counts on can be cleared away while its main patent is still in force.

It has been revealed that with no extra years to work with, Astellas changed the product instead. It got new Xtandi tablets listed for reimbursement in April, ahead of the generics, which rolled out only as capsules. It also priced the stronger 80mg tablet so a month of treatment costs about 25% less than the same dose in 40mg capsules, which means fewer pills to swallow and a smaller bill.

That edge may not last. Generic makers have already applied for approval of their own tablet versions.

The question now is whether a more convenient pill and a lower monthly cost can keep Korean patients on the brand once cheaper copies come in every form.

#179177. ‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ opens to $120 million despite GTA VI—and its audience explains why

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (647 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy 📈 Bullish 🌐 Fortune ↗ Open Full Page

‘Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping’ opens to $120 million despite GTA VI—and its audience explains why

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (647 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fortune

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to an estimated $120 million in North America this weekend, nearly three times the $44 million debut of its 2023 predecessor, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes.
  • It did so in the shadow of Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited Rockstar Games release that arrived one day earlier.
  • Recent findings suggest that in hindsight, releasing a Hunger Games movie the day after GTA VI may have been a clever piece of counterprogramming.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping opened to an estimated $120 million in North America this weekend, nearly three times the $44 million debut of its 2023 predecessor, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes. The Lionsgate prequel added $105 million overseas for a $225 million global launch, returning the franchise to the three-figure heights of its original run.

It did so in the shadow of Grand Theft Auto VI, the long-awaited Rockstar Games release that arrived one day earlier. Fans and industry insiders alike speculated that the game, which topped $1 billion in pre-sales ahead of its Nov. 19 launch, would monopolize the attention economy and drain an already thin November box office.

Recent findings suggest that in hindsight, releasing a Hunger Games movie the day after GTA VI may have been a clever piece of counterprogramming. “I think the marketplace has already spoken,” Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian told the Associated Press.

Both GTA and The Hunger Games are now multigenerational action franchises, but the former has always targeted men, mostly young-adult to 40-year-old gamers drawn to its edgy depictions of criminal violence. The Hunger Games, meanwhile, has its roots in teen readers and women.

It has been revealed that like the five films before it, Sunrise on the Reaping is adapted from Suzanne Collins’s young-adult novels. It centers on 16-year-old Haymitch Abernathy, played by Joseph Zada, but the series was built around its heroine, Katniss Everdeen. Jennifer Lawrence, who led the original four films as Katniss, returns for a brief epilogue cameo.

The opening-weekend audience bears out the split. Women made up 67% of ticket buyers, and 74% were between ages 18 and 34, according to the AP. Lionsgate studied the risks of opening against GTA from the earliest stage of dating the film and concluded the two could coexist.

While the Mature-rated GTA VI may have kept men of a certain age glued to their consoles this weekend, the PG-13 Sunrise on the Reaping held on to the core Hunger Games crowd: young women, along with teens too young to play the game.

That base may also have come out of thirst for a massive-screen, four-quadrant blockbuster. This fall has been a sleepy season for PG-13 action movies, with dramas, documentaries, and R-rated fare dominating the box office and the zeitgeist. Audiences liked what they found: The film earned an A- CinemaScore, up from the B+ that greeted Songbirds & Snakes.

In a recent development, overall, the weekend was a surprisingly strong one for theaters. Total domestic grosses topped $160 million, nearly double the prior weekend, though still about 10% below the same frame last year, when Wicked: For Good opened.

Recent findings suggest that sunrise on the Reaping accounted for most of that. Behind it on the weekend chart came I Play Rocky with $9.3 million in its first weekend of wide release, Ebenezer at $7.7 million, and The Cat in the Hat at $6.9 million. You Can See Everything is still hanging in the top 10, adding another $2.5 million.

These titles are diverse, but most target an audience different from GTA VI. Beyond The Hunger Games locking up young women, I Play Rocky is for the boomer dads, and The Cat in the Hat is for kids.

In a recent development, if you’re connected to me on LinkedIn, we’ve talked. That’s on purpose. I get a lot of requests, but I don’t connect just to connect.

According to recent reports, my filter is simple: a thoughtful note, or a profile that makes me curious. When someone clears that bar, I message them, introduce myself and suggest a 15-minute intro call by phone or Zoom. You can call me while you’re commuting, cooking dinner or taking a walk. That sentence is the whole lesson. In PR, we talk about earned media versus paid media. Relationships work the same way. Trust that someone else earned with you and passed along is the most powerful credential you’ll ever have, and no ad can buy it.

Being picky pays off here, too. Over the years, the people I know well have become my own personal advisory board.

I share the latest in health and wellness, including my own protocols, along with business tips and a little joy. Readers tell me it feels like a note from a friend, which is exactly the point.

Sources indicate that people now reach out because of what I post. The content does the introducing for me. By the time we get on that 15-minute call, they already know what I care about, and the conversation starts three steps ahead.

Treat your network like your most important client. Be selective. Be generous. Show up as a human.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 19, 2026 at 6:33 pmNovember 19, 2026 at 6:33 pm.

Redmond, Wash.-based RBC Signals has announced a $10 million strategic growth investment aimed at accelerating the tech giant’s expansion into government satellite data services and the commercialization of emerging space technologies.

RBC Signals supports satellite operators by arranging access to a global network of ground stations, including its own assets and antenna facilities operated by partners.

In August, for example, Blue Origin and RBC Signals confirmed a partnership to build out the ground infrastructure for Blue Origin’s Quartz communications network. RBC Signals is also a provider for the U.S. Space Force’s Joint Antenna Marketplace.

The newly unveiled investment was led by Washington Harbour Partners, a private investment firm based in Washington, D.C. The firm ranked sixth among all defense technology investors in the Silicon Valley Defense Group’s 2026 NatSec100 Report.

“Our vision has always been to build a global, secure network of networks that makes space connectivity more accessible, flexible and reliable,” Ron Faith, RBC Signals’ president and CEO, mentioned today in a news release.

According to recent reports, “By bringing together infrastructure, partners and emerging technologies, we’re creating a dual-use platform that can evolve alongside the needs of the national defense and the commercial space industry,” Faith said. “This investment from Washington Harbour Partners will help us accelerate that vision by expanding our government services business and bringing emerging capabilities such as higher frequency bands, optical connectivity, intersatellite links and space domain awareness to market.”.

Mina Faltas, founder and CEO of Washington Harbour Partners, highlighted RBC Signals’ role in addressing the growing demand for space connectivity. “We see tremendous potential in the company’s ability to deliver mission-critical capabilities, and we’re excited to support the team as they enter this next phase of growth,” Faltas said.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, fanatics has become a one-stop shop for sports fans looking to rep their favorite teams and athletes.
  • For cofounder and CEO Michael Rubin, however, the road to building that empire nearly ended before he turned 20.
  • Rubin caught the entrepreneurial bug at just 12 years old, when most kids are more concerned with middle school homework than starting a business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, fanatics has become a one-stop shop for sports fans looking to rep their favorite teams and athletes. But the firm has grown into a powerhouse in its own right, striking partnerships with nearly every major U.S. sports league, including the NFL, NBA, and MLB, and generating roughly $14 billion in annual revenue.

For cofounder and CEO Michael Rubin, however, the road to building that empire nearly ended before he turned 20.

Rubin caught the entrepreneurial bug at just 12 years old, when most kids are more concerned with middle school homework than starting a business. By 13, he was selling ski equipment out of his parents’ basement in Pennsylvania, and a year later, he had opened his own storefront just down the road from his home. He was making money quickly—and even went in with his friend in buying a Porchse before he could even legally drive.

But in around 1988, there was an unusually warm winter, and so his customers weren’t coming.

According to recent reports, “It didn’t snow that year,” Rubin recalled in a recent conversation with podcaster David Senra. “End of the year, I had $200,000 of bills, $80,000 of inventory, and I was sitting right in front of bankruptcy.”.

To get himself out of the hole, he negotiated his debts down to $35,000, went door to door borrowing money from neighbors, and used the proceeds from a newly introduced venture in the closeout business to repay his loan within three weeks. Five years later, at 21, Rubin was generating $150 million in sales buying and selling closeout merchandise.

“I went from death in its eyes, bankrupt, thought I was complete failure, giving up on entrepreneurship, to five years later, doing $150 million, making $10 to $15 million a year as a kid,” Rubin said. “And so to me, each disaster, if you learn from it, leads to your next success.”.

Rubin spent just one semester at Villanova University before dropping out to focus on business. He continued building his sports merchandise operation, KPR Sports, which eventually became part of Global Sports Inc., later renamed GSI Commerce.

As the internet took off, Rubin shifted the business toward e-commerce, helping major retailers and sports teams sell merchandise online.

According to recent reports, but the 2008 financial crisis nearly wiped him out again. Rubin had borrowed heavily against his GSI stock, which lost roughly 90% of its value during the bear market. He began calling a friend who managed a hedge fund, where Rubin had invested $5 million, repeatedly asking for his money back. After roughly 100 calls, he finally got it—with just hours to spare before the bank could seize his shares.

The business eventually rebounded and was bought by eBay in 2011 for $2.4 billion. As part of the deal, Rubin bought back the firm’s sports e-commerce business, laying the foundation for today’s Fanatics.

The tech giant has since grown into a giant valued at $31 billion in 2022, while Rubin’s personal fortune has grown to an estimated $11.6 billion, according to Bloomberg.

Still, Rubin stated he wouldn’t trade the ups and downs that got him to his level of success today.

“I liked the adrenaline of fighting for my life,” Rubin stated.

It has been revealed that “If it’s the same shit every day, it’s boring,” he added. “Business is a rollercoaster. Business is an adventure. If you’re a real entrepreneur, you like that. You thrive on that.”.

Fortune reached out to Fanatics for further comment.

Rubin isn’t the only successful business leader to have nearly lost it all at a young age.

In the early days of Ray Dalio building out his now-multibillion-dollar hedge fund business, he was broke living in Latest York City—and had to ask his father to borrow $4,000 to help cover bills.

The experience gave him humility, but also made him develop a deep respect for those who do fail—and embrace the lessons learned.

“Anyone you see succeeding is only succeeding at the things you’re paying attention to—I guarantee they are also failing at lots of other things,” Dalio wrote.

In a recent development, “The people I respect most are those who fail well. I respect them even more than those who succeed. That is because failing is a painful experience while succeeding is a joyous one, so it requires much more character to fail, change, and then succeed than to just succeed.”.

It has been revealed that mark Cuban has echoed that failure is an inevitable part of building a successful career. On his path to a $9.8 billion net worth, he made countless early missteps—from trying to sell powdered milk to getting fired from jobs and making bad investments. It’s the ability to not let them define any entire career is what matters.

“No one is going to know or care about your failures, and neither should you,”  he noted. “All you have to do is learn from them.”.

"Will wait for Bitcoin bottom again," Kiyosaki noted.

The financial educator reminded his followers of one of his notable investment tips.

"Your profit is made when you buy….not when you sell," Kiyosaki noted.

Basically, the financial educator suggested that investors should prioritize finding good entry prices rather than trying to buy Bitcoin while its price keeps dropping.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that five factions appear in the final Avengers: Doomsday trailer, from the X-Men to Wakanda and Talokan. See what each brings to the alliance.

It has been revealed that superhero crossovers once meant a single team assembling, but Avengers: Doomsday puts many teams side by side, with heroes drawn from different films, studios and even universes. The crowd is so large that one of its founding heroes cannot place half of it. "I don't know what half of you do. I don't even know who half of you are. Put aside your petty squabbles. The time has come. Team up and stand together," Thor says in the final trailer, as reported by Screen Rant. The greater danger is less any single villain than the chance that rival factions cannot fight as one.

Recent findings suggest that marvel is betting that audiences want every thread pulled together at once, and fans have already shown that appetite. When Avengers: Endgame returned to theaters as the Encore re-release, fans around the globe paid another $143 million to see it, according to Variety. Fans watched the Doomsday trailer 503 million times in its first 24 hours, according to Yahoo Entertainment. Every faction Marvel adds comes with its own fans, each with a reason to buy a ticket, and that explains why the studio packs in every team it can.

Ars Technica identified the superhero factions that appear in the Avengers: Doomsday trailer. They range from the veteran mutants of Fox's earlier X $TWTR-Men films to the twin kingdoms of Wakanda and Talokan and a Fantastic Four from another universe. The final trailer is the last look audiences get before the film opens in theaters Dec. 18, and the question is not only who indicates up but what each faction brings to a fragile alliance.

Sources indicate that the Avengers gave the whole franchise its name, and that is why the condition of this team matters more than any other in Avengers: Doomsday. The Avengers of Earth-616 rank first among the factions in the trailer, according to Ars Technica, yet the man who anchors them had to be fetched. Yahoo Entertainment reports that the trailer highlights the Fantastic Four arriving at Steve Rogers's home to recruit him. The core that greets him is a reunion of old partners rather than a team that kept working together, pairing Steve with Sam Wilson and with Bucky Barnes, who last appeared in Thunderbolts in 2025.

Steve had found the ending he wanted, and the film reopens it on purpose. He has a teenage son with Peggy Carter, Yahoo Entertainment reports, and in the trailer the boy apparently doesn't know his father was a superhero. "We sort of played one beat past where Steve Rogers's story ended with Peggy Carter," codirector Anthony Russo noted. That makes Steve a symbol the whole alliance can rally to, and also the member with the most reason to walk away.

In a recent development, even inside the core team, the old roles have changed hands. Sam Wilson holds the title of Captain America, and Steve returns to lead the team beside him, with Thor in the ranks as well. The team that carries the franchise name now has two men with a claim to lead it.

The Avengers bring the weight of history to this crowd, but they are leading an alliance before they have finished rebuilding their own team.

Industry observers note that marvel is bringing an entire team from another film series into Doomsday rather than borrowing one familiar face for a cameo. The veteran mutants from the earlier X $TWTR-Men movies return with their shared history intact, according to Ars Technica. Patrick Stewart again plays Prof. Charles Xavier and Ian McKellen again plays Magneto, Variety reports, and audiences have connected those two actors with the series more than anyone else in its cast. "Original" here means the first roster of that film series, the actors who defined these mutants on screen. What this faction adds to the crowd is instant recognition.

The X-Men also arrive as a full squad rather than a few stray members. James Marsden is back as Cyclops, and Kelsey Grammer returns as Beast, Rebecca Romijn as Mystique and Alan Cumming as Nightcrawler. Alongside the six returning actors, Marvel added Channing Tatum as Gambit, the one newcomer on the team. A team with this much history together can fight as a unit from its first scene, but mutants who have long stood together may look to one another before they look to an Avenger.

The X-Men arrive as the most complete team in the film, already assembled under their own banner, and that is why they will be the hardest to absorb into anyone else's.

The Fantastic Four of Earth-828 come to Avengers: Doomsday from a different universe than the Avengers of Earth-616. The family of heroes leaves its own universe to warn the others that worlds are about to collide, according to Ars Technica. That warning is the reason they belong in this crowd. The Avengers learn how large the threat is from a team none of them grew up with. Before any alliance can form, they have to trust strangers.

The Fantastic Four deliver their warning in person. In the trailer, Screen Rant reports, the team reaches Steve's home, he leaves his family behind to go with them, and Thor arrives alongside them. In a crowd that is short on trust, heroes from another universe are doing the work of assembling the Avengers.

Even the location of Steve's home remains uncertain. Screen Rant writer Simon Gallagher places it on Earth-828, the Fantastic Four's own universe. That placement is his reading of the trailer and not a confirmed plot point. If he is right, the Fantastic Four are familiar figures in that household, because Steve's son recognizes them, and they would be neighbors calling on a retired hero, not strangers carrying news.

Whatever their motive, the Fantastic Four are turning a warning into a roster, and the open question is whether a crowd of rivals will follow a team from outside their world.

Marvel is putting its newest team into the crossover almost as soon as that team exists. The Thunderbolts, now billed as the New Avengers, are one of the five factions in the final trailer, according to Ars Technica, and their roster includes Florence Pugh as Yelena, Wyatt Russell as U.S. Agent, David Harbour as Red Guardian, and Hannah John-Kamen as Ghost. Yahoo Entertainment reports that audiences have not seen the group since the Thunderbolts film, so the team has had little time to settle into its roles.

The name "New Avengers" places this group beside the original team rather than beneath it. The overlap reaches down to single heroes. The newcomers have their own Falcon, played by Danny Ramirez, Yahoo Entertainment reports, while Anthony Mackie's Sam Wilson stands with the core Avengers. The heroes on the field now answer to two groups that claim the same title.

In a recent development, the Newly introduced Avengers add fresh faces and more fighters. They also raise an open question about which team the Avengers name now belongs to.

In a recent development, wakanda and Talokan have the most crowded teaser of any Doomsday faction, even though the two kingdoms come fifth of the five factions, according to Ars Technica. ComicBook.com reports that their own teaser features five main characters, while the first two teasers revealed two each and the X $TWTR-Men's showed three. A studio usually gives its fullest teaser to the heroes it expects audiences to care about. Marvel appears to be counting heavily on these kingdoms, whatever their place in the order.

Recent findings suggest that wakanda arrives with power divided between two people. Shuri fights as Black Panther, but M'Baku rules as king of Wakanda, according to ComicBook.com. The nation's champion and its ruler are now different people, and both a warrior and a king will have a say in what Wakanda commits to the alliance.

In a recent development, talokan sends a delegation, and its ruler is the faction's biggest open question. Namor comes with Attuma at his side, and the Wakanda teaser, ComicBook.com reports, gives the first confirmation that Namora is in Doomsday. Two kingdoms in one faction give the alliance more fighters, and also more leaders whose aims have to line up. The idea of Namor siding with Doctor Doom remains speculation, and Doom does not appear in the Wakanda teaser.

The last faction shows how much a crowded alliance gains when it adds a kingdom, and how much the alliance depends on whether one ruler stays.

Right now, companies are interacting with customers who are not giving up, losing their patience after being put on hold or missing what’s in the fine print of the business’s policies. That’s because these customers aren’t humans. They’re personal AI agents acting on behalf of humans.

It has been revealed that meta’s Muse and xAI’s Grok Bot are the two getting the most attention right now. Muse skyrocketed up to number one in the App Store, and Meta’s stock jumped double digits in the same week. Financial markets have been trying to price what these personal agents mean for retail, travel and banking. Massive corporations are already reacting, with Amazon blocking Muse outright and Shopify electing to build Muse its own checkout lane instead.

There’s a lot of noise right now about what these personal AI agents should and will be allowed to do. The dust has clearly not settled, and some very important questions hang in the air. But make no mistake: This will not be a passing trend or a footnote in the broader story of AI innovation. This is a massive shift in how businesses interact with customers, and the companies that start getting ready for it now are the ones who will be prepared when it arrives at their front door.

From the consumer’s perspective, a personal agent fights the battles they don’t want to, and does so more rigorously than they ever could.

Industry observers note that someone’s flight gets cancelled, and their personal agent can argue with the airline until it gets a credit. Someone points it at subscription services and gets every one to offer a discounted rate. I’ve seen dozens of these examples pile up on social media over the past few weeks, and the pattern is always the same. A task a person would normally decide was not worth the trouble is now getting done anyway, because an agent has no concept of trouble.

We used to think about bots talking to bots like something that will happen “someday.” It’s happening now. For consumers who don’t want to solve problems through sheer persistence and patience, this is an exciting development. For businesses that have built their customer service programs around interacting with humans, this is a challenge to solve, fast.

The simple response to this innovation sounds like: “We need our policies to be accurate, because AI will be better at calling us out on them than a human customer.” It goes deeper than that. Every refund policy and guarantee clause has fine print and phrases that are ever so slightly open to interpretation. Personal AI agents can read these policies and find where they bend in ways a human never could.

And they’ll do this at scale. One customer raising a question and finding a loophole is a cost of doing business. Thousands of agents doing the same thing can overwhelm a business, both financially and operationally.

That kind of volume does not behave like a normal surge in customer support demand. It behaves more like a denial-of-service attack. Nobody debates whether each individual request is legitimate; the volume itself is the problem. The response has to be infrastructural: detecting, filtering, a real system for deciding what gets through. “We will deal with it when it happens” is not a strategy at this scale.

Retail and travel may seem like the industries most vulnerable to risk, but any business with documented policies faces the same exposure. Insurance, financial services, healthcare — wherever a organization has put a promise or statement of intent in writing, an agent can find it and act on it.

AI has already carved out a massive role in how businesses interact with customers. Now it’s showing up on the other side of the conversation. Nobody has every single answer for how to prepare for this upcoming reality, us included. But there are foundational moves worth making now, rather than waiting for the rest of the industry to decide what to do.

First, there’s the question of identity. Most businesses have no reliable way to know whether they are talking to a customer, a customer’s authorized agent or something pretending to be one. That infrastructure needs to be in place before anything else matters.

Second, you need visibility into what is already happening. You need to be able to see how often an agent is showing up in a support queue, what it’s asking for and how often it’s succeeding.

Then there’s the concern of the policies themselves. A traditional review to ensure accuracy is no longer sufficient. Businesses need to audit their policies, line by line, and stress-test every potential ambiguity that could turn into a vulnerability. Find the gaps before an agent does.

Search engines that tried to wall off the open web lost to the ones that stayed open, and the same pattern is likely to repeat here. Open does not mean undefended. It means building real verification and governance instead of a blanket “no,” even while the rest of the playbook is still being written.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In July, Tesla posted a video of a 93-year-old San Diego resident named Lois using a red Tesla equipped with Full Self-Driving (FSD) Supervised software to make road trips to see her family and run errands.
  • “I don’t have to wait for someone, and it’s been a wonderful experience,” Lois remarked to the camera after a video montage of her visiting her grandkids and smiling at the beach.
  • It has been revealed that tesla has promoted FSD Supervised, which can change lanes and make turns, as a way for seniors to keep their independence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In July, Tesla posted a video of a 93-year-old San Diego resident named Lois using a red Tesla equipped with Full Self-Driving (FSD) Supervised software to make road trips to see her family and run errands.

“I don’t have to wait for someone, and it’s been a wonderful experience,” Lois remarked to the camera after a video montage of her visiting her grandkids and smiling at the beach.

It has been revealed that tesla has promoted FSD Supervised, which can change lanes and make turns, as a way for seniors to keep their independence. The manufacturer is now rolling out a fresh version of the software. Reposting another video in March of an 87-year-old woman testing out an FSD-equipped Cybertruck, the company said “FSD Supervised can give you back your freedom.” Elon Musk has also said that Tesla self-driving “enables safer mobility for senior citizens” on X.

But Tesla’s promise comes with a catch: FSD Supervised still requires a driver to monitor the road. Tesla added “Supervised” to the name after California regulators accused it of misleading customers about what the software could do. That raises a safety dilemma for older drivers who are turning to FSD Supervised as their driving abilities decline. Tesla itself has cautioned that none of FSD Supervised’s features can replace an attentive person at the wheel, which is why some legal experts question marketing it to older drivers. Lawyers say the pitch could expose Tesla, too: a federal jury has already found the tech giant partly liable for a fatal crash involving Autopilot, its more basic driver-assistance system.

“A technology that requires a capable driver to supervise it should not be marketed as a magical mobility solution for drivers who aren’t capable of safely driving without it,” Angel Reyes, a personal injury attorney based in Texas, told Fortune.

Sources indicate that FSD Supervised could be dangerous for older drivers because it depends on them being able to spot and react quickly to hazards. A study by University of Iowa researchers last year found drivers ages 75 to 84 were more likely to be responsible for crashes involving right turns compared to drivers ages 45 to 64, which the researchers remarked may be related to reduced physical flexibility or worsened eyesight. The same age group was also more likely to be at fault in crashes at traffic signals, which may be due to declining vision or slower reaction times, the study’s lead author said.

Recent findings suggest that “The seniors who would benefit most from a car that drives itself are often the ones least able to supervise one,” Brian White, a personal injury trial lawyer who deals with car crashes, told Fortune. “If someone is relying on it because of slower reactions, vision loss or memory problems, those same limits make them a poor backup for the software.”.

According to recent reports, tesla has faced some scrutiny over its automated-driving tech. Fortune previously reported its robotaxi fleet in Austin had been involved in 14 crashes over 800,000 miles driven, or one crash for every 57,000 miles, which was about eight times the average crash rate of American drivers recorded by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. Traffic signals are also where FSD has drawn federal scrutiny: the NHTSA also started investigating Tesla last year over instances of its FSD-engaged cars running red lights and “driving against the proper direction of travel on public roadways.”.

The agency initially identified six reports of crashes involving an FSD-engaged Tesla running a red light and colliding with other cars in the intersection. Four of those crashes resulted in one or more reported injuries. The investigation will look at “whether there was prior warning or adequate time for the driver to respond to the unexpected behavior or to safely supervise the automated driving task.”.

Sources indicate that white noted there’s a liability risk for Tesla if its FSD Supervised marketing makes older drivers put too much trust in it. He cited a potential legal precedent for this: A Miami jury ordered Tesla to pay $243 million last year after finding its driving-assistance tech Autopilot partly responsible for a fatal crash. A federal judge upheld the verdict in February, though Tesla has appealed.

“A company that markets a feature in a way that leads people to trust it too much can share responsibility,” he noted.

Tesla did not respond to Fortune’s requests for comment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 20, 2026 at 7:52 amNovember 20, 2026 at 9:14 am.

According to recent reports, orchard Robotics, an agtech tech giant using artificial intelligence to help growers monitor crops and make farming decisions, has been acquired by John Deere. The deal was confirmed Thursday and the terms were not disclosed.

Recent findings suggest that the startup has developed a system of cameras mounted on tractors and other equipment that gather images as the machines traverse a farm. Orchard’s AI analyzes the images to generate data on vines, trees and crops, which is then used to track growth, yield and health.

“This acquisition connects crop-level intelligence with John Deere technology and equipment that can precisely execute the work in the field,” Tim Marquis, John Deere’s director of farm systems innovation, said in a statement.

That includes helping farmers target treatments and make better-timed decisions about thinning, spraying and harvesting.

Orchard was founded by CEO Charlie Wu, a Thiel Fellow who dropped out of Cornell University to launch his business in 2022.

In a recent development, “Over these next few years, our goal is to bring the power of Orchard’s industry-leading technology and AI Farming capabilities to every farmer out there,” Wu noted in a LinkedIn post. “This is only the beginning of a long and awesome journey ahead.”.

According to recent reports, the startup is based in San Francisco and has an office in Seattle. Wu splits his time between the two cities and was a finalist for Young Entrepreneur of the Year at the 2026 GeekWire Awards.

In a recent development, orchard has raised more than $25 million from investors, including a $22 million Series A round confirmed in September 2025. The startup has 45 employees, according to PitchBook.

The Pacific Northwest is home to numerous agtech startups. That includes other companies that collect and analyze data, such as Loftus Labs and innov8.ag, as well as IUNU and Koidra, which are focused on greenhouse crops. Businesses tackling field operations include weed destroyers Carbon Robotics and Aigen; rock-removing TerraClear; and irrigation startups FarmHQ and Verdi.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re like me, your approach to nutrition mostly involves squinting at a label, not recognizing any of the ingredients, and eating the thing anyway. Peter Castleman decided that wasn’t good enough. After four decades as an investor, including as Chairman and Managing Partner of J.H. Whitney & Co., where he played a role in investments tied to The North Face, Igloo and Herbalife, Peter came out of retirement to become the founder and CEO of WISEcode, an AI-powered food transparency platform that has mapped more than 840,000 products. He’s 70 years old and states he’s never felt more excited about an idea, proving it’s never too late to chase a big idea.

Give us the elevator pitch. What is WISEcode?Basically, we’re trying to solve what I call the food information crisis. We literally don’t know two things: what’s in our food and what it does to us. At WISEcode, we’ve been spending a dozen years or so solving that. We’ve created what we call the Food Genome Project, which is really mapping the entire food system. So we now know exactly what’s in our foods, and we can tell you what it does for you. And that applies to consumers, policymakers, government people, industries, retailers, scientists, everyone. That information didn’t exist, and now it does.

It has been revealed that this isn’t the first tech giant you’ve started or been a massive part of. Why did you want to become a founder again?Well, I’m 70, okay? When I turned 50, I retired from my firm. I’m healthy. I eat generally well. But when you turn 50, you enter the kill zone for chronic disease, and chronic disease is 90% of our health problems, and 80% of chronic disease is driven by what we choose to do. We actually control most of our health outcomes. So I basically wanted to simply hack what I’m going to eat. I didn’t want to get cognitive issues. I didn’t want to get any late-onset chronic disease. But that hack doesn’t exist. It shocked me. It just doesn’t exist. So this passion became the business purpose of WISEcode, and I said, “Okay, I’m gonna get this information. I’m going to do for me, I’m going to do for every single individual. I’m going to give them Food Truth.” Formally, I’ve probably been doing this for about 12, 13 years. Informally, I’ve been thinking about it for 20 years.

When a business is a personal passion, do you have a process for figuring out whether it will be a passion for other people, too? Or do you just follow your heart?Like many people, I suffer from that latter part, which is letting your emotions get too far into stuff. I’ve always stated, “Fall in love with your family and your friends, not your businesses.” It’s hard to do, because you develop passions. I have three tests I generally apply to any kind of activity. The first I call the North Star test: is it very clear that what you’re trying to do resonates with others? Is it going to be an aha moment or a so-what moment to the world? Number two, I call the sandbox test. How substantial is your sandbox? How big is your addressable market? And how crowded is your sandbox? And then the third one I call the moat test, which is: can you build defensible business assets that prevent people from copying what you do? People will copy you in a second if you’re successful. If I’m not slam-dunk strong on all three tests, I try to stay away. I apply that to WISEcode. I apply it to everything I do. I’m better at it now than I was at 25.

How do you figure out if other people are interested in your idea when you don’t have a significant budget?Social media and everything we have today are double-edged swords. But I use SurveyMonkey all the time. You can ask a question and, for not very much money, you can get 500, 1,000 really clear answers that help you evolve. You can do the same thing on social media tools. The tools out there today are so great. It used to be you’d have to hire McKinsey or Bain for a gazillion dollars, and they’d do a six-month study. Now, in a day, you can get better information than they ever gave you.

What do you say to someone in their 50s who thinks, “I always wanted to do my own thing, but it’s too late”?First and foremost, I think you gotta be honest with yourself. Who are you? What do you love doing, and are you good at this? Late in your career, any time, if you don’t have the energy, the drive and the staying power, don’t do it. Because building companies is hard. You’re going to get knocked on your fanny a ton of times. You gotta get back up. You gotta inspire others around you. You gotta keep going when everyone states, “Don’t do it.” You’re gonna run out of money. You’re gonna have your spouse saying, “What the hell are you doing?” But if it’s in your DNA, it’s the greatest thing in the world. Most of my contemporaries are reducing their handicap on the golf course, and I’m spending 10 hours a day, seven days a week on WISEcode, and I love it. I wouldn’t change it for the world, but that’s me. The greatest joy I get, besides my love of my friends and family, is building businesses that actually make a difference, and if that’s in your DNA, do it. I think the only failure in life is not trying.
